articles.title: When Politics Enters the Waiting Room: Far-Right Electoral Victories Exacerbate Discrimination in Access to Healthcare
articles.authors: MERLIN SCHAEFFER, ALESSIO ROMARRI, DINA ROSENBERG, KRZYSZTOF KRAKOWSKI
articles.abstract: Far-right political shifts have been linked to increased racism, raising concerns about their impact on minority access to public services. This study investigates whether far-right electoral victories encourage discrimination by street-level bureaucrats, who are expected to act impartially. We conducted a nested research design in Italy, combining a field-experimental audit with a regression discontinuity design focused on municipalities near the electoral threshold for far-right mayors. Research assistants with native-Italian and West-African accents contacted municipal healthcare offices to request registration with a general medical practitioner. Compared to native-Italian callers, those with West-African accents faced significantly higher rates of scrutiny and dismissive responses. Leveraging close elections, we find that this disparity was exacerbated in municipalities where far-right candidates narrowly won. These findings demonstrate that far-right electoral success can undermine impartiality and equal access to essential services.

articles.title: Economic Self-Interest and Support for Redistribution: New Evidence Using Election Results Data
articles.authors: JIEUN LEE, E. GRANT BALDWIN, G. AGUSTIN MARKARIAN, BENJAMIN J. NEWMAN
articles.abstract: A formidable corpus of scholarship explores the role of economic self-interest in shaping public support for redistribution. One striking feature of this literature is its near-exclusive reliance on reported preferences in surveys, with little-to-no research analyzing revealed preferences in the form of actual voting on redistribution. Leveraging eight redistributive ballot initiatives across six American states and a total of 73,053 observations of revealed support for redistribution, we uncover consistent evidence that the economic standing of precinct voters is systematically related to their support for redistribution. We find that lower- to upper-middle-income precincts are each significantly more supportive of redistribution than upper-income precincts, with pronounced decreases in support associated with the increasing prevalence of high-income households subject to proposed tax increases. Finally, we observe the largest class differential in support for redistribution in more heavily Republican precincts.

articles.title: Globalization and the Hinterland: International Trade and the Rural–Urban Divide
articles.abstract: The growing political divide between rural and urban regions is often attributed to rural deindustrialization and import competition in manufacturing. Yet this cleavage emerged in many countries well before rural industrialization, pointing to underlying economic forces that existing accounts have overlooked. We argue that comparative advantage in agriculture is one such force: rural voters are more likely to support protectionist parties and policies when local agriculture is uncompetitive, since this sector is often central to their communities’ economic and social life. Using a new harmonized dataset of surveys from 123 countries and extensive data on voting behavior in the European Union, we find strong support for our argument. An additional analysis exploiting exogenous subnational variation in agricultural competitiveness in the United States post-NAFTA further corroborates our findings: the political divide between rural and urban voters is pronounced in uncompetitive regions but negligible in those possessing a comparative advantage in agriculture.

articles.title: What Do “Most People” Believe? Race, Gender, and the Generalized Other
articles.authors: Natasha Quadlin, Trenton D. Mize, Long Doan, Bianca Manago
articles.abstract: When people form beliefs in social life, they often calibrate their own thinking against what they anticipate “most people” think. Although prior research demonstrates the importance of these inferences, scholars have yet to examine who is best proxied by “most people.” Given persistent inequalities in U.S. society that advantage White men, as well as theories of cultural hegemony, we hypothesize that “most people’s” imagined beliefs are closely proxied by those of White men. We test these ideas using an original survey experiment conducted with a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults ( N = 2,089) in which we adapt 64 core items from the General Social Survey. Respondents were randomly assigned to answer these questions either from the perspective of most people, or from the perspective of designated race-gender groups. Contrary to our hypothesis, we find strong and consistent evidence that White men are not seen as standard-bearers for most social issues. Instead, perceptions of what most people believe are highly aligned with the imagined beliefs of White women. Importantly, this pattern emerges not because White women are seen as influential, but because White women are perceived as less extreme than other groups. We also observe variation across respondents, such that respondents tend to center their own race-gender group in conceptualizing most people’s beliefs (with White women typically close behind).

articles.title: Simply a Sign of the Season? Christmas Trees as Cultural Ciphers in Local Government Management of Diversity
articles.authors: Gary J. Adler, Damon Mayrl, Eric Plutzer, Jonathan S. Coley, Rebecca Sager, Elise Wolff
articles.abstract: How do local governments symbolically manage the diversity of their residents? Drawing from an original representative sample of local government officials, we use a novel survey experiment with open-ended survey responses to examine preferences for cultural objects that symbolically manage religious diversity, an axis of difference that is increasingly salient to social conflict. Our experiment randomly varies the content of holiday displays on government property to measure diversity management strategies. Results show that government officials prefer the assimilationist strategy of a Christmas tree—by itself—over multiculturalist and exclusivist strategies, which both include sectarian religious content. Officials also evaluate Christmas trees as the content least likely to signal government endorsement of religion, compared to other holiday displays. We argue that these patterns can be explained by conceiving of a Christmas tree as a cultural cipher, a well-known cultural object that affords a range of meanings and resonates across social identities as innocuous. We argue that cultural ciphers are useful for an assimilationist approach to managing diversity because their ambiguity allows them to act as a vehicle of symbolic inclusion while also sustaining the meanings of majority groups. We also consider how cultural ciphers may lose their power for civic solidarity.

articles.title: Incentivizing Equality? How Work-Family Policies Affect Parenthood Penalties in 27 Countries
articles.abstract: Work-family policies are theorized to shape the division of paid labor after parenthood, but recent studies have cast doubt on their importance. Leveraging harmonized longitudinal data spanning 27 countries and an analytic focus on couples and couple dynamics, our study shows that work-family policies do shape how divisions of paid labor change with parenthood, and that they also moderate the importance of couples’ relative resources as a determinant of the division of labor. We find that moderate-length paid maternal leave and greater childcare availability reduce parenthood penalties in couples’ division of paid work time, while prolonged leave exacerbates penalties. Furthermore, by focusing on couples, we provide novel evidence that partners’ relative resources do not operate uniformly across work-family policy contexts, showing that policies can incentivize couples to divide paid work in ways their relative resource profiles would not otherwise predict. We find that moderate-length paid leave and greater childcare availability encourage egalitarianism among male-breadwinner couples, although extended leave encourages greater gender traditionalism among female-breadwinner couples. These findings reveal that classic theories of household specialization and bargaining are not universal, and highlight the need for greater theoretical attention to how country- and couple-level forces interact to shape gender inequality.

articles.title: Geoengineering, Moral Hazard, and Disrespect
articles.abstract: Scientists and policy makers are increasingly exploring solar geoengineering as a tool for combatting anthropogenic climate change. Yet these technologies have drawn intense ethical criticism. One of the most influential critiques – the ‘moral hazard’ objection – holds that pursuing solar geoengineering risks undercutting mitigation efforts; and that, as a result, governments should halt the development of solar geoengineering. This paper argues that the moral hazard objection faces a dilemma: either the proposed solution to the moral hazard effect (that is, stifling geoengineering) is unnecessary, or it expresses a morally troubling form of disrespect. Articulating this dilemma serves three purposes. It shows, first, that the moral hazard objection is substantially more difficult to vindicate than it initially appears. Second, it clarifies what would need to be shown, empirically, to overcome this ethical hurdle. Finally, and crucially, it sheds light, more broadly, on what it means to respect people’s agency when designing and implementing public policies.

articles.title: National Narratives in Comparative Politics: Theories, Methods, and Insights From Asia
articles.authors: Dean Dulay, Eun A Jo, Paul Schuler
articles.abstract: In this introduction to the special issue, we define and explore the concept of national narratives in East and Southeast Asia. First, we define national narratives as collectively shared stories about a nation’s origins, boundaries and purposes. Second, we discuss three undertheorized elements of the narrative: the identity of the storyteller, the content of the stories, and contestation over the dominant narrative. Finally, we assess some methodological and measurement challenges in the literature before introducing the papers in this special issue. Drawing on cases from China, Vietnam, Indonesia, South Korea, Taiwan, Myanmar and the Philippines, we address questions related to the construction of personality cults and colonial memory. We also discuss how democratization impacts the identity of the storytellers, and how this impacts views on national boundaries and political violence.

articles.title: State-Building at What Cost? The Consequences of Military Control in Medieval China
articles.authors: Joy Y. Chen, Erik H. Wang
articles.abstract: A key challenge to state-building in conflict-prone societies is the proliferation of autonomous armed actors. As governments seek to enhance their monopoly over violence, consequences of military centralization deserve scholarly attention. We argue that centralization undermines state’s coercive capacity: by weakening the leaders of armed groups, it simultaneously erodes the military efficiency and discipline of these groups, which also serve as agents of coercion for the state. We leverage a centralization reform in China’s Tang Dynasty (618-907 CE) after a civil war, using unique data on soldier mutinies, rebellions by local generals, civilian uprisings, and battle outcomes. Difference-in-differences estimates reveal that centralization successfully reduced local generals’ rebellions, but led to increased soldier mutinies against the generals and more civilian uprisings. It also worsened battlefield performance. While research on state capacity has focused on its extractive and administrative dimensions, these findings deepen our understanding about another important aspect: the coercive dimension.

articles.title: Bulwarks or Enablers? Political Elites’ Attitudes to Political Candidates with Armed Group Linkages
articles.authors: Juan Diego Duque-Salazar, Hanne Fjelde, Sandra Håkansson
articles.abstract: Many elections feature candidates with ties to violent groups, yet little is known about the nomination stage. To understand whether political elites serve as gatekeepers against such candidates or whether other desirable traits lead selectors to overlook violent linkages, we study selectors’ preferences in candidate selection. Using an experiment with 11,392 Colombian local political elites, we examine how alleged armed group collusion is weighed against experience, track-records, popular support, and endorsements. We find that candidates with rumored armed group ties face a significant penalty in selectors’ evaluations. Some attributes, particularly experience, reduce this penalty, but none fully offset it. Candidates with ties to armed groups are also less rewarded for strong performance, suggesting that violent linkages diminish returns to otherwise desirable qualities. These findings indicate that the prevalence of violence-linked candidates is not primarily driven by selectors’ willingness to accommodate them, redirecting attention toward concealed linkages and constrained candidate pools.

articles.title: Incubating Revolution: How Social Networks and the Built Environment Sustain Mobilization
articles.abstract: How do challengers sustain mobilization under conditions of extreme repression? Social networks and the built environment are critical, interacting at two time scales. Settlement, chain migration, and everyday cooperation produce dense relational environments that shape motivations and constitute latent resources. When contention erupts, those dense social networks can be repurposed to sustain high-risk collective action, providing shelter, escape routes, information, and support. But their efficacy is limited without the organic built environment in which they form; its proximity, limited visibility, and constrained access amplify the effect of dense social ties in facilitating challenge under threat. We substantiate these claims using disaggregated data on protest in Damascus during the 2011 Syrian uprising, finding that neighbourhoods with both dense networks and organic built form exhibit significantly more frequent and confrontational mobilization. By analytically separating the social from the spatial, this article illuminates the mechanisms through which urban neighbourhoods become incubators of rebellion.

articles.title: Trade-Offs in Authoritarian Participatory Digital Surveillance: Evidence From China’s Sharp Eyes Project
articles.abstract: How do authoritarian regimes overcome the limits of digital surveillance? They complement camera systems with citizen monitoring and reporting, creating participatory surveillance in which residents interpret what cameras capture and supply local knowledge technology alone cannot provide. I study this hybrid form of control in China’s Sharp Eyes Project, which gives selected residents access to camera feeds and encourages reports of suspected misconduct. I use a staggered difference-in-differences analysis of administrative and survey data from Chinese cities. The program increases citizen reporting by 11%, reduces crimes susceptible to community monitoring, and lowers trust in neighbors. Reports expand the state’s informational reach, but the system makes residents uncertain about how neighbors may interpret and report their behavior. The study places political participation at the center of digital surveillance and shows how authoritarian regimes turn relations among citizens into a source of state power while weakening the foundations of collective action.

articles.title: Policy Interpretation and Implementation: Expanding Abortion Access in Latin America
articles.abstract: This article explores the role of social movement activists in policy implementation. I introduce the mechanism of interpretation: by influencing how providers interpret policy mandates and apply discretion, or by directly providing services themselves, activists may expand service delivery beyond formal law. I present a paired comparison of the abortion rights movements in Colombia and Argentina to show how two distinct groups of activists and providers expanded access to abortion via a similar pathway. In Colombia, elite professionals diffused knowledge from the top-down, and in Argentina, activists and healthcare providers worked independently and in grassroots networks. This work has implications for our understanding of how policy is implemented, how real-world outcomes can diverge from original policy intent, and how activists can expand service provision and rights recognition when their access to formal institutions is constrained.

articles.title: Motherhood and Constraints during Job Search
articles.abstract: Why do women’s labour earnings drop upon motherhood? We shed new light on this question by analysing the changes in job search behaviour associated with motherhood. We exploit data on the job applications sent on a popular online platform linked with administrative registers for 350,000 involuntarily unemployed workers in France. After losing their job, mothers have a 11.7% lower probability to find a job than similar women without children and send 12.2% fewer job applications. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we analyse the timing of job applications. Unlike other women, mothers’ rate of applications decreases by about 20.5% in the hours when there is no school. Moreover, the French reform that introduced school on Wednesday in 2014 led mothers to send more applications on Wednesdays. Our results highlight that childcare creates constraints on the timing of job search activities for mothers. We finally provide suggestive evidence that these constraints decrease their return-to-search, and thereby contribute to their lower application and job finding rates.

articles.title: Union Membership and Native-Immigrant Labour Market Gaps
articles.authors: Samuel Dodini, Alexander Willén, Julia Li Zhu
articles.abstract: We estimate the causal effects of union membership on labour market outcomes for natives and immigrants, exploiting quasi-experimental variation from large increases in Norway’s tax deduction for union dues. Union membership raises earnings and improves employment protection for native workers, while the private returns for non-Western immigrants are substantially smaller and often close to zero. Complementary survey evidence suggests that this gap is not explained by differences in information, preferences, or engagement with unions: immigrants receive similar information when joining, report similar preferences over job amenities, and are more likely than natives to seek union assistance. Instead, the combined administrative and survey evidence is consistent with differences in union-side behaviour. Immigrants report lower satisfaction after contacting unions for support and are more likely to believe that native workers and those with strong local networks receive greater benefits from membership. The impact is most pronounced in concentrated labour markets, indicating that relying on unions to address monopsony-based market failures may unintentionally amplify group inequalities.

articles.title: Free to Fail? Paternalistic Preferences in the United States
articles.authors: Björn Bartling, Alexander W Cappelen, Henning Hermes, Marit Skivenes, Bertil Tungodden
articles.abstract: This paper examines paternalistic preferences in two large-scale experiments with participants from the US general population. Participants decide whether to intervene when a stakeholder is about to make a choice misaligned with the stakeholder’s own preferences. Willingness to intervene depends on which intervention is available: only a minority implements a hard intervention, which restricts the stakeholder’s choice set, while a majority implements a soft intervention that provides information without restricting choice. A substantial share of participants does not defer to the stakeholder’s stated preferences when evaluating welfare. Our framework estimates that about half are welfarists and a third libertarian paternalists.

articles.title: From # ExpelUngratefulAfghans to # ExpellingAfghansIsANationalDemand ; A Comparative Analysis of Digital Xenophobia and Anti‐Migrant Hate Campaigns in Iran and Pakistan
articles.abstract: This paper examines the rise and function of anti‐Afghans immigrant digital movements in Iran and Pakistan, specifically #افغانی_نمک_حراموں_کو_بھگاو (#ExpelUngratefulAfghans) in Pakistan and #اخراج_افغانی_مطالبه_ملی (‘Expelling Afghans is a national demand’) in Iran, focusing on their development and impact from 2023 to 2025. Drawing on a mixed‐methods approach that includes discourse analysis, social network mapping and policy review, the study traces how coordinated hashtag campaigns have constructed Afghan migrants as existential threats to national identity, security and economy. These campaigns—often driven by small but hyperactive networks—do more than reflect public sentiment; they contribute to a discursive climate that may reinforce state‐led deportation drives, legal restrictions and securitized migration policies. By comparing digital hate ecologies in both countries, the study reveals converging patterns of bottom‐up xenophobic mobilization and top‐down amplification by state and media actors. This research offers a rare cross‐national perspective from the Global South on how online xenophobia reshapes migration politics in authoritarian contexts.

articles.title: Segregated Spaces, Shared Lives: A Mixed Inquiry Into Afghan Immigrant Settlement in Iran
articles.authors: Leila Zandi‐Navgran, Hossein Afrasiabi, Rasoul Sadeghi, Abbas Askari‐Nodoushan
articles.abstract: Immigrant residency and settlement remain contentious issues in destination societies. This study examines the residential perceptions and patterns of Afghan immigrants in Iran, addressing two central questions: What mechanisms and conditions influence the residential patterns of immigrants? How do immigrants perceive their residential circumstances? Using a Concurrent‐Embedded Mixed‐Methods approach, data were collected through fieldwork with 55 participants and supported by secondary sources. This design gathered qualitative and quantitative data simultaneously, with the quantitative insights embedded within the qualitative analysis. The categories identified from the analysis include: centralization, concentration, unevenness, immigrant‐dependent economic sectors, interpersonal and social boundaries, bonding/bridging social capital, civic and cultural participation, socio‐economic status, legal and policy constraints and settlement duration. Together, these categories point to residential segregation as the core category. The findings show that at the national level, Afghan immigrants are predominantly concentrated in major cities and metropolises due to state residential policies. At the regional level, they also settle mostly in provincial capitals due to government policies regulating the allocation of migrants. Locally, their concentration is highest in specific neighborhoods—often on the urban periphery—driven by socio‐economic conditions, social ties and duration of stay.

articles.title: Europe Needs Filipino Workers: A Leverage for the Philippines?
articles.authors: Maruja M. B. Asis, Bernard Allan Garcia, Eunice Tejada
articles.abstract: Compared to the established labour migration corridors between the Philippines and destination countries in Asia and the Gulf region, recent moves by European countries to recruit Filipino workers to meet current and future labour needs invite reflection on what this emerging trend implies for migration knowledge and theorising about migration, particularly the aspect of migration governance. As a relatively new terrain of engagement for both origin and destinations, this paper focuses on how key stakeholders from the Philippines view this growing trend: (1) how do different migration‐related stakeholders in the Philippines see the increasing demand for Filipino workers in Europe; (2) what kinds of engagements are developing between the Philippines and European countries on labour migration issues; and (3) what specific issues pose challenges for migration governance in the Philippines‐Europe labour migration corridor. Data for this paper come from expert interviews with participants from Philippine government institutions ( n = 3), private recruitment agencies ( n = 3), non‐government organisations ( n = 3), and Philippines‐based representatives of European destination countries ( n = 2). The findings add to the growing literature on origin states, open insights on their role in bilateral relations with destination countries, and how origin countries can leverage their resources to reduce power asymmetry vis‐à‐vis destination countries.

articles.title: Beyond the Battlefield: Localized Civilian Clashes and Political Attitudes in Violent Conflict
articles.authors: Carly Wayne, Sivan Hirsch-Hoefler, Masanori Kikuchi, Daphna Canetti
articles.abstract: In protracted conflicts, civilians frequently encounter low-level, hostile actions from adversary civilians in nearby communities, yet the political consequences of these events remain understudied. We investigate this question in the Israeli–Palestinian context, examining how community-level exposure to hostile actions by Israeli settlers shapes Palestinian political attitudes in the West Bank. Leveraging a novel data set containing thousands of geo-coded conflict events from 2010 to 2020 paired with forty-six Palestinian public opinion polls in the West Bank, we find that district-level increases in settler hostilities are significantly associated with heightened political militancy among local Palestinians, associations that are larger and more robust than those from local Israeli military actions. A second empirical strategy examining changes in Palestinian attitudes before and after the establishment of nearby settler outposts reveals that this form of civilian land expropriation likewise leads to modest increases in political militancy among Palestinians in proximate towns. These findings highlight the distinct political impact of localized, low-level civilian actions and territorial expropriation—central but often overlooked features of sectarian territorial conflicts—offering insights for territorial and ethnic disputes globally.

articles.title: When Firms Lead States: Financial Intermediaries and the Politics of Sovereign Green Bond Issuance
articles.abstract: Sovereign green bonds typically appear only after corporate green bond issuance has accumulated—a sequence at odds with the policy consensus that sovereign borrowing anchors debt market development. I argue that the inversion reflects market building by global investment banks. The four banks that authored the Green Bond Principles in 2014 used early private corporate transactions to build the verification practices, pricing conventions, and investor networks needed for a functioning market, then served as lead managers when sovereigns entered, transferring accumulated expertise across the public–private divide. States entered a market whose institutional infrastructure they did not design. The Cox proportional hazards model shows that accumulated corporate issuance significantly accelerates sovereign entry, while government agency issuance delays it by substituting for direct sovereign participation. A bank-level triangulation shows that founding-bank presence at sovereign entry reflects green-bond-specific expertise transfer rather than general dominance in sovereign debt underwriting. The findings identify financial intermediaries as a distinct channel through which sustainable finance reaches sovereign borrowers and show how privately constructed market conditions shape the terms on which states engage with global climate finance.

articles.title: The Weight of the Law: How International Law Affects Foreign Policy Preferences
articles.abstract: Studies have shown that international law can influence attitudes toward foreign policy. We know less about how law exerts this influence. We develop four theoretical models to explain how international law affects foreign policy attitudes. Drawing on survey experiments with 4,900 US citizens about arming a foreign government involved in a civil war, we find some support for three of the models: When respondents are told that sending arms would be illegal, they are more likely to believe that the United States would (1) face sanctions, (2) break a commitment, and (3) contribute to harmful moral outcomes. We also examine whether international law amplifies these concerns beyond the effects they might have without international law. We find that sanctions reduce support more strongly when they result from violating international law than when they result from ordinary political retaliation by other states. However, illegality does not strengthen the effects of violating commitments or causing harmful moral consequences. This suggests that international law primarily shapes public opinion indirectly. Rather than serving as an independent reason to oppose a policy, violations of law draw attention to moral and practical concerns that citizens might otherwise overlook.

articles.title: Making Sense of Disrupted International Order
articles.abstract: The apparent turmoil in the US-led liberal international order has left international relations scholars without a settled framework for explaining—or teaching—global governance. This Special Section addresses that gap by developing subsystems theory as an analytical approach for understanding change and continuity in an interdependent, contested international order. Subsystems—collections of state and nonstate actors organized around a single core governance question—offer a more disaggregated unit of analysis than the “issue areas” central to regime theory, allowing analysts to identify variation in strategic benefits and punishments for noncompliance that issue-area-level frameworks obscure. We situate subsystems theory alongside other post-regime-theory approaches, particularly regime complexity and weaponized interdependence. We argue that subsystems theory offers complementary analytical leverage, especially for tracing de facto cross-issue interactions and nonstate behavior. The Section’s three articles apply this framework to election monitoring, international finance and antitrust enforcement, and oil sanctions and maritime safety, demonstrating the theory’s utility across strikingly different empirical domains. Read together, the articles illuminate two concepts central to any theory of global governance—punishment and participation—and show how multiple, subsystem-specific international orders, rather than a single liberal order, increasingly characterize world politics.

articles.title: Economic Statecraft Trumps Ideology: Experimental Evidence on US Sanctions against Chinese Investment
articles.abstract: How does US economic statecraft shape public attitudes toward Chinese investment in third countries? As great power competition intensifies, middle powers face increasing pressure to align their economic relationships with geopolitical demands. How these pressures translate into policy depends critically on public opinion, yet we know little about how citizens in targeted countries respond to economic coercion. Using a pre-registered survey experiment conducted in Chile, we provide the first experimental evidence that US sanctions threats significantly reduce support for Chinese investment in a potential target country. Sanctions threats reduce positive evaluations by over 40 percentage points, a dramatic shift that persists across ideological groups, including left-leaning respondents typically skeptical of US influence. These findings suggest that, under conditions of credible economic threat, concrete costs can override abstract geopolitical loyalties, challenging theories that emphasize the primacy of ideological filters in foreign policy preferences. Our results speak to broader debates about economic statecraft effectiveness, demonstrating that threatened costs can reshape public preferences before any economic pain materializes, even among citizens predisposed against the sanctioning power.

articles.title: Breaking the Conflict Trap: Nonviolent Mobilization and the Recurrence of Civil War
articles.abstract: We argue that large-scale nonviolent mobilization in post-civil war settings reduces the likelihood of conflict recurrence by diffusing a pluralist political culture and by incentivizing governments to respect political civil liberties, a process conceptualized here as horizontal democratic norm diffusion and vertical democratic norm change, respectively. Using causal mediation analysis and an instrumental variable approach with data from V-Dem and the Phoenix Historical Event Dataset, this study shows that post-conflict nonviolent mobilization lowers the risk of civil war recurrence through its positive effects on societal pluralism and governmental respect for political civil liberties. These findings contribute to the literatures on nonviolent resistance and peacebuilding by demonstrating the peace-promoting potential of nonviolent mobilization in post-civil war contexts and by clarifying the mechanisms through which it influences the recurrence of armed conflict.

articles.title: The Medieval Peace Dividend: Post-Alfredian Anglo-Saxon State Formation, Political Networks, and Peace
articles.authors: Eric Grynaviski, Jittip Mongkolnchaiarunya, Sverrir Steinsson
articles.abstract: Prominent theories of state formation hold that the origin of the state is rooted in warfare. Heightened insecurity incentivized rulers to develop institutional innovations in taxation, administration, and military organization. Emerging evidence from the medieval world, however, suggests a more complex picture. Early royal governments were tiny and had relatively small resource bases. During the early periods of state formation, existential security threats might divert the kinds of resources needed to enact comprehensive state reform. We refer to this as a security-reform tradeoff. Existential security threats can divert attention and resources away from comprehensive state reforms. We examine patterns of state formation in post-Alfredian Anglo-Saxon England, from the end of the ninth century to the late eleventh century, measuring political centralization using prosopographic data. We find a relationship between periods of peace and political centralization. We examine the causal mechanisms through a comparative case study of four Anglo-Saxon kings’ reigns.

articles.title: Historical Border Changes and Contemporary Public Health Outcomes
articles.authors: David B Carter, Matthew Gabel, Alma Velazquez
articles.abstract: Trust in government is a key predictor of adherence to government recommendations and accordingly plays a central role in compliance with public health policies. The COVID-19 pandemic underlined the importance of voluntary adherence to government public health recommendations. How trust deficits might be overcome to increase public health compliance depends crucially on its sources. We argue that the legacies of state-building and international politics in Europe are a significant source of variation in contemporary local adherence with public health recommendations. Building on research that links historical border changes to trust deficits in Europe, we show that more border changes in a locality relative to neighboring units affects two public health outcomes in Europe: COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy during the 2021 vaccine rollout and uptake of three established vaccines prior to the pandemic. We show that trust in government mediates the relationship between border instability and uptake of these established vaccines at the local level.

articles.title: When it’s your own child: effects of media narratives on U.S. parents’ support for their LGBTQ+ teen
articles.abstract: Parents’ responses to their LGBTQ+ child are varied, often intense, and have important consequences for the child. To examine how media depictions may shape responses, a pre-registered online experiment of 494 parents tested effects of viewing two TV narratives, depicting either control (non-LGBTQ+) family interactions, parental rejection, gradual growth toward acceptance, or unalloyed acceptance, of a lesbian or transgender teen, on parents’ support and behavioral intentions regarding their own LGBTQ+ teen. Guided by theories of vicarious contact and inspiring media, we assessed mediation via identification with characters, and via feelings of inspiration and manipulation, testing baseline support as a moderator. Effects of condition were indirect-only, and contingent on baseline support. Among highly supportive parents, growth and acceptance narratives (vs. control) increased feelings of inspiration, which predicted positive behavioral intentions. Among less supportive parents, rejection and (unexpectedly) growth narratives reduced identification with depicted LGBTQ+ teens, indirectly decreasing support and behavioral intentions.

articles.title: The integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring: a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ hate speech
articles.authors: John P Crowley, Elizabeth A Hintz, Amanda Denes
articles.abstract: Social support is a fundamental human need and communication process. Yet, scholars theorizing about social support have been limited by several pervasive assumptions: (a) people are able to recruit support when needed, (b) others are willing and able to provide support, (c) what counts as “good” support is mutually understood and desirable, and (d) support seeking is binary and static. Researchers must productively move beyond these assumptions to enhance the depth and breadth of theorizing about the process of support seeking. By addressing these assumptions and consolidating the literature concerning support seeking and marshaling, we set forth the novel, field-general integrative theory of supportive network (re)structuring (ITSNS) grounded in the interpretive paradigm. To accomplish this, we introduce process theorizing, forward three propositions forming the ITSNS’ heuristic framework, and offer criteria for evaluating the ITSNS. Finally, to illustrate the utility of the ITSNS in research practice, we offer a case study in the context of LGBTQ+ people seeking support following an experience of hate speech.

articles.title: Presenting the Updated Non-State Actor Dataset
articles.authors: David E. Cunningham, Leo Bauer, Olivia Bauer, Kristian Skrede Gleditsch, Idean Salehyan
articles.abstract: This data feature presents an update (Version 4.0) to the Non-State Actor (NSA) data, which provide information on the characteristics of rebel groups in all state-rebel group dyads in the Uppsala Conflict Data Program/Peace Research Institute Oslo Armed Conflict Dataset (ACD). The previous version of the NSA data ended in 2011, and Version 4.0 extends coverage through 2024, adding more than 250 new dyad spells and aligning pre-2011 data with Version 25.1 of the ACD. The added period is a consequential one for the study of conflict: the number of conflicts and conflict fatalities have risen substantially, while international conflict management efforts have declined. We describe the coding process and present descriptive analyses showing marked increases in rebel strength relative to the government and in rebel territorial control over the post-2011 period. We also discuss applications of the data to research on rebel governance and violence against civilians, two areas where scholarship has grown substantially since the data were last updated. The update further allows the range of data projects built on the NSA to be extended, supporting research on how the changing character of contemporary conflict shapes its dynamics and outcomes.

articles.title: Parliamentary Elites in Authoritarian Regimes: new data
articles.abstract: Authoritarian politics are largely defined and shaped by elite politics. Yet, our knowledge about political elites in nondemocracies remains confined to those in particular regimes or, cross-nationally, leaders at the highest echelons of decision-making. This article introduces a novel dataset, Parliamentary Elites in Authoritarian Regimes (PEAR), that fills this gap and provides comprehensive information on members of parliament (MPs) across nondemocracies. With currently more than 230,000 observations on individual MPs from 882 legislative terms in 133 authoritarian regimes from 1945 to 2024, PEAR is based on the largest individual-level demographic database on national legislators ever assembled and provides unprecedented information about these types of elites in authoritarian regimes. The dataset records MPs’ names, gender, age, party affiliation, incumbency status, and constituency, and uniquely classifies legislators into ruling-party members, regime-supporting elites, and opposition politicians. These are then aggregated into legislature-level variables in the country-year format, showing, for instance, the share of women in parliament, the MPs’ mean and median ages, the share of young and elder MPs, and legislatures’ retention rates. I first present how the dataset was created from publicly available sources, including parliamentary websites, electoral commissions, and election observer reports, then highlight descriptives, and validate it against existing datasets. I then illustrate an application of the data, generating new insights into the reshuffling of elites in authoritarian regimes. PEAR will be an invaluable resource for our understanding of autocracies.

articles.title: The impact of drone warfare on suicide bombings in Pakistan
articles.abstract: Drone strikes against militant groups have become a central counterterrorism tool, yet their effectiveness remains debated. We use weather-based instruments and a major drone-base closure to identify the causal effect of Central Intelligence Agency drone strikes in North Waziristan, Pakistan, on suicide bombings nationwide during 2008–2016. Our instrumental variables strategy improves on recent work by combining cloud cover interacted with precipitation—which directly impedes camera-based targeting—with a base closure providing qualitatively different variation. Focusing exclusively on suicide bombings allows us to test specific theoretical mechanisms and provide evidence no existing study offers: quantification of the total programme effect, heterogeneity between decapitation and non-decapitation strikes, and systematic analysis of attack target types. We find each drone strike causes approximately one additional suicide bombing within the subsequent month, with 18%–23% of all suicide bombings during this period causally attributable to the drone programme. Strikes eliminating militant leaders provoke reactions roughly 8 times stronger than ordinary strikes. These reaction attacks predominantly target security installations, not civilians, contradicting theories emphasizing capacity loss or undisciplined violence and instead supporting our proposed mechanism: militant groups strategically “green light” pre-prepared suicide attacks as face-saving responses to authority challenges. We formalize these predictions as four testable hypotheses—blowback effects, decapitation amplification, strategic targeting, and rapid response—all of which receive empirical support. Our findings complement recent evidence that drone strikes increase terrorism and that leadership targeting disrupts organizational control, while providing novel evidence on suicide bombing dynamics, decapitation heterogeneity, and strategic target selection. The results suggest policymakers should anticipate month-long vulnerability windows after strikes, particularly following leadership kills, and harden security targets rather than assume militants will shift to softer civilian targets.

articles.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision
articles.authors: Heejung Jung, Hunar Jain, Xiaochun Han, Ma Feilong, Jane Han, Deepanshi Shokeen, Cara Van Uden, Isabella Hanson, Andrew C. Connolly, Tor D. Wager, James V. Haxby, Samuel A. Nastase
articles.abstract: Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

articles.title: Heterogeneous impacts of temperature extremes on climate attitudes and Green voting
articles.authors: Jacopo Bassetto, Roman Hoffmann, Raya Muttarak, Jonas Peisker, Piero Stanig
articles.abstract: In the past decade, the public in Europe has become more concerned about climate change and expresses stronger proenvironmental policy preferences. Based on data from the European Social Survey (2012–2022, 25 countries), we show that the increased exposure to temperature extremes has contributed to the observed changes in climate change attitudes and electoral support for environmentalist policy platforms. For each additional degree of excess temperature experienced during warm spells measured over the previous 12 mo, we find that the probabilities of being worried about climate change, of feeling responsible for climate change, and of voting for Green parties and Green coalitions increase by 4.0 [CI95: 2.5, 5.5], 2.5 [CI95: 1.1, 3.9], and 2.8 [CI95: 0.9, 3.7] percentage points respectively. We also document significant heterogeneity across individuals, based on gender and education, particularly between highly educated women and low-educated men. While the latter group consistently exhibits the lowest proenvironmental attitudes and voting, it is this group that shows the strongest increases when exposed to temperature extremes, converging toward the levels of their more educated counterparts. Further regional heterogeneity analyses reveal that the effects of warm temperature extremes are smaller in less prosperous or economically disadvantaged regions, as well as in regions with greenhouse gas emission levels above the median. The findings suggest a nuanced interplay between individual factors and contextual influences in shaping climate attitudes of European citizens and their motivations or reservations toward greater climate action.

articles.title: Equity dimensions of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards: Long-term spatial population projections for New York City consistent with Shared Socioeconomic Pathways
articles.authors: Deborah Balk, Jenna F. Tipaldo, Leiwen Jiang, Hamidreza Zoraghein
articles.abstract: Projections of future population are important for a myriad of reasons. Large cities, states, and countries routinely produce near- and mid-range population projections. In the context of climate change, the Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP) framework is used at global and national scales to project long-term population to inform future emissions scenarios and understand future climate-related exposures and impacts. Much less consideration has been given to long-term projections at smaller scales, even though climate impacts are place based and cities now host most of the world’s population. Cities and their metropolitan regions are complex, heterogeneous in terms of population, environmental, and built features. Thus, using global or national-scale approaches overlooks important aspects of urban futures. Cities are diverse, fluid population centers home to migrants, with employment opportunities yet substantial inequality. These quintessential city-centric features are ignored in global/national-scale population projection methods, including long-term ones consistent with the SSPs. Leveraging state-level SSP-based projections, here we extend that approach for New York City, currently home to 8.8 million persons. Combining multistate and multiregional demographic projection and spatial downscaling models, we project county-level population by racial/ethnic groups and age–sex to 2100 and downscale to 100 m. Such projections allow for an equity lens to inform assessments of future vulnerabilities to climate hazards. Four of the five SSPs project that the population of New York City will be smaller and much older at the end of the century, though these futures are dependent on demographic assumptions about fertility and especially migration.

articles.title: Polarising punchlines: The influence of intergroup humour on affective political polarisation
articles.authors: Yara Sleiman, Maria Grasso, Charles Pattie, Laura Serra, Carlo Hofer
articles.abstract: How does political humour influence affective polarisation? In today’s media landscape, humour is increasingly used to ridicule political opponents, potentially deepening partisan divides. At the same time, humour may mitigate polarisation by evoking positive emotions and softening reactions to political critique. To date, it remains unclear whether intergroup political humour affects polarisation differently from equivalent non-humorous content. We address this question using a survey experiment in Great Britain ( n = 2011 ) with a 2×3 factorial design varying in message tone (humorous or non-humorous) and target (in-group, out-group or non-political). We find that serious in-group criticism increases affective polarisation, as measured by trait-based evaluations. Notably, this effect is significantly attenuated when the same messages are delivered humorously. Humour, therefore, reduces polarisation in situations that would otherwise provoke defensive reactions among group members. Mediation analyses provide suggestive evidence that this effect operates through increased message discounting and reduced negative emotional responses.

articles.title: Gaining confidence – Examining the effects of participation in deliberative mini-publics on self- and other-regarding democratic beliefs
articles.authors: Frederik Pfeiffer, Tim M. Daw, Vera Telemo
articles.abstract: Research on the participation effects of deliberative mini-publics has often focused on political opinions and knowledge, but less is known about the effects on confidence in deliberation and political talk. Given widespread concerns about eroding tolerance and trust in democracy, deliberation should ideally contribute to citizens’ ability to engage in political talk, as well as the confidence that such talk is possible and worthwhile. Following Dahl’s strong principle of equality, we argue that it is important that citizens believe that other people are capable of contributing. Thus, this study asks whether participation in mini-publics fosters confidence in political talk, measured by internal political efficacy, confidence in others’ democratic abilities and tolerance for opposing views. Using before–after surveys from three Swedish mini-publics in 2024, we find significant increases in participants’ confidence in their own abilities and those of co-participants, despite high baseline values. Effects on perceptions of people in general and tolerance for disagreement were mixed. When comparing cases, we find stronger effects when participants had more deliberation time and when the issue of the assembly was more politicised. The findings suggest that mini-publics can enhance confidence in political talk, depending on their design, duration and context.

articles.title: Does policy align with the preferences of the affluent because they are better informed? An empirical test
articles.authors: Sirus Håfström Dehdari, Jesper Lindqvist, Anders Sundell
articles.abstract: Research shows that affluent citizens see more of their preferred policies realized than the less affluent. If indicative of unequal influence over decisions, then this poses a problem for democratic equality. But one theory suggests that the affluent are better informed and therefore prefer policies that were going to be implemented anyway. If so, it would be a question of unequal information, not influence. We test this theory on the case of monetary policy in the United Kingdom, where information effects are especially likely: The policy-maker (the Bank of England) has a well-defined goal of price stability, there is broad expert agreement on how to achieve this, and the general public is not well informed of inflation dynamics. Survey data from more than 120,000 UK respondents from 2001 to 2026 reveal that monetary policy aligns more with the preferences of high-income earners, who are better informed about monetary policy and the state of the economy. Nevertheless, information can only explain about a quarter of the gap in preference–policy alignment between income groups, even in this most-likely setting. The unequal policy alignment identified in previous research is therefore unlikely to be a mere artifact of informational asymmetry and remains an important problem for political equality.

articles.title: Dueling Political Fictions and Public Administration and Democracy in an Era of Populism and Authoritarian Impulses
articles.abstract: The political fictions used in political discourse, during the English Civil War period, remain relevant to contemporary public policy and administration. Mainstream public administration discourse has too often employed the fiction of a singular and unbounded popular sovereignty that emerged during this period, leaving public administration ill‐equipped to deal with the authoritarian impulses of contemporary populist governments. What is needed in public administration discourse, in dealing with these authoritarian impulses, is not an ethic of administrative neutrality, such as has traditionally dominated much of our field, but an ethic of constitutionalism that draws on the fiction of the individual that was also articulated during the English Civil War period by the English Levellers and subsequently by the founders of the American Constitution.

articles.title: Do Gender-of-Interviewer Effects Differ Across Immigrant Generations? Survey Evidence from Italy
articles.abstract: Interviewer gender has been shown to affect responses to survey questions on gender attitudes and norms, but does its influence vary across groups with different migration backgrounds? I study this question using the Between Origin and Destination (BOnD) survey, conducted in Lombardy, Italy, between 2024 and 2025. Consistent with gender-of-interviewer effects, a type of social desirability bias, female interviewers elicit more progressive responses on a summary index of gender norms and on an index of the acceptability of homosexuality, abortion, divorce, casual sex, and premarital sex. The effect is concentrated among natives and second-generation individuals; first-generation immigrants show little response to interviewer gender. One possible explanation is that social desirability pressure from a female interviewer operates through host-country social norms: Individuals more embedded in the Italian normative context are more responsive to cues from a female interviewer. These findings have implications for the design of surveys administered to mixed native-immigrant populations.

articles.title: Investigating the Utility of LLM-Based “Silicon Samples” in Political Science Conjoint Experiments
articles.abstract: This research note is the first study to explore the viability of using LLM-generated respondents in forced-choice conjoint experiments. I generate naive “silicon samples” using three models, GPT 4o-Mini, Llama 3.2, and Magistral-small-2506, benchmarked to a large sample of live conjoint respondents, allowing for direct comparisons between human and silicon choices. The resulting analyses suggest that naively generated silicon samples are insufficient to simulate human decision-making in conjoint tasks; these results also suggest that there are systemic differences in the way demographic covariates shape LLM and human choices in experimental contexts. In total, this analysis makes two important contributions: it establishes a descriptive baseline understanding of LLM-generated respondent performance in conjoint experiments and suggests that naive silicon samples cannot accurately infer human choices using demographic traits in experimental decision making contexts. Finally, the implications of these results imply that LLMs consider covariates differently than live respondents do in micro-level decision making contexts.

articles.title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-led Interviews
articles.abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. We assess its robustness by drawing comparisons to human experts and with several respondents-based quality metrics. The versatility of the approach is illustrated through four broad classes of applications: eliciting key factors in decision making, political views, subjective mental states, and mental models of the effects of public policies. High performance ratings are obtained in all of these domains. Our applications highlight the potential of AI-led interviews as a tool for measurement, hypothesis generation, and discovering mechanisms.

articles.title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
articles.abstract: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.

Religion and early fertility in the United States: changes during the second demographic transition
articles.authors: Jeremy E Uecker, Riley S Peterson
articles.abstract: We assess how changes in early fertility varied among US women with different religious characteristics, and how the associations between religion and early fertility changed across birth cohorts from 1950 to 1993. Using data from the National Survey of Family Growth, we examine the timing of nonmarital, marital, and overall first births through age 24. Results from life tables and discrete-time event history models reveal that increases in early nonmarital first births were smaller among women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood, whereas early marital births declined at similar rates irrespective of childhood religious service attendance. Because early births became increasingly nonmarital across birth cohorts, women who attended religious services more frequently in childhood became less likely to have an early birth overall. Early fertility differences by religious tradition generally converged across cohorts, although women raised conservative Protestant continued to have higher likelihoods of early birth relative to women raised in other religious traditions net of controls. Women who were raised nonreligious remained similar to conservative Protestants in their likelihood of nonmarital childbearing across cohorts and became statistically similar to them in their overall early births in the latest cohort. Changes in early fertility during the second demographic transition therefore varied by religious background and reshaped the relationship between religion and early fertility.

Beyond economic bargaining power? Work-related internal migration and subjective well-being in couples
articles.authors: Elias Hofmann, Nico Stawarz, Nicolai Netz, Heiko Rüger
articles.abstract: Bargaining theory posits that both partners’ utility shapes couples’ migration decisions. Yet, most empirical tests focus on individual incomes, thus overlooking non-economic factors in couples’ deliberations about spatial mobility. We argue that considering holistic indicators of utility, such as subjective well-being, can advance our understanding of couples’ decision-making. Using data from the German Socio-Economic Panel (SOEP, 1991–2021) and fixed effects panel regressions, we analyze changes in life satisfaction following work-related internal migration on both individual and dyadic levels. Moreover, we examine whether these changes depend on shifts in partners’ economic bargaining power (EBP, defined as female partners’ share of total household labor income), thereby evaluating the common assumption that couples’ bargaining centers around income. Our results show that, on average, both partners experience increases in their life satisfaction following migration. Distinguishing whether women’s EBP remains unchanged, decreases, or increases with migration, we find that women’s life satisfaction gains are only weakly related to changes in their EBP. In contrast, men’s life satisfaction only increases if their partner’s EBP decreases or remains unchanged, but not if it increases—a pattern consistent with the notion of gendered expectations about the within-couple income distribution hampering men’s well-being gains. Overall, our findings suggest that well-being is an important factor in couples’ migration decision-making and that income-based measures of bargaining power provide only an incomplete account of partners’ bargaining positions.

articles.title: What Do Mini‐Publics Prove?
articles.abstract: Lottocracy is a novel political arrangement that replaces elected politicians with ordinary citizens selected at random. It is unlike any political system that currently exists, so it is natural to have anxiety about how it would work in practice. To mollify these concerns, many lottocrats point to the successful performance of mini‐publics as evidence that lottocracy would work well, if tried. This inference resembles a claim about external validity, I argue, and develop a framework for evaluating it by relying on work from the social sciences and philosophy of science about when such claims are warranted. With this framework in hand, I show that mini‐publics teach us little about how lottocracy would work in practice, although the strength of this conclusion depends on which specific version of lottocracy is under consideration. Mini‐publics, however, do provide evidence about the abilities of ordinary citizens more generally, undermining some of the strongest claims about their lack of political competence. The framework developed here applies to a broader class of arguments in political philosophy: arguments that use the performance of existing institutions to predict how similar but untried institutions would perform.

articles.title: How to Talk with the Academic Community about Contested Knowledge: A Confrontational-Reflexive Interview Model
articles.abstract: Interviewing academics about contested knowledge presents significant methodological challenges, as the interview situation often activates “official” professional repertoires that conceal ambivalence and the active construction of epistemic boundaries. To address these limitations, the authors propose and evaluate the confrontational-reflexive interview model (CRIM), a research design aimed at systematically eliciting reflexivity and analyzing boundary-work in situ . The model treats the interview not as a neutral information extraction tool but as a structured sequence of meaning-making occasions. Stage 1 establishes a baseline narrative in expert interviews and focus groups, which is subsequently disrupted by a standardized “confrontation stimulus”—a scholarly text explicitly challenging the dominant disciplinary consensus—forcing participants to negotiate their position against a credible internal critique. Stage 2, conducted approximately one month later via asynchronous written correspondence, introduces temporal distance to test the stability and revisability of these accounts outside the immediate pressure of the face-to-face interaction. Drawing on a study of political scientists’ discourse on conspiracy theories, the authors demonstrate that although standard interviewer probes often fail to unsettle “official” narratives, the combination of a third-party textual confrontation and delayed reflection successfully reveals the specific conditions under which experts reproduce, repair, or redraw the boundaries of legitimate knowledge. The authors argue that CRIM contributes to sociological methodology by offering a replicable framework for observing expertise as a contingent, interactional performance.

Learning traps
articles.abstract: When constituents are uncertain about whether leaders' policy preferences align with their interests, policy choices generate a trade‐off between payoffs and information. Leaders can experiment with their preferred policy, but if the outcome is bad, constituents learn this and threaten office removal. I use a repeated model of political agency to analyze how this trade‐off shapes long‐lived, term‐unlimited leaders' policy choices. When there is uncertainty about the optimal policy for constituents, leaders implement “learning traps”: spatially intermediate policies that halt learning about what the best policy is. They experiment only when their preferences are very likely to be aligned with constituents, a contrast to the “gambling for resurrection” logic ubiquitous in the literature. I provide a case study that examines how the 1861 reforms ending Serfdom in Imperial Russia represented the logic of a “learning trap” and illustrate additional applications of the model to political contagion and economic policymaking.

articles.title: The threat‐enhancing effect of authoritarian power sharing
articles.abstract: Power‐sharing deals can potentially solve the autocrat's commitment problem, yet often fail to prevent conflict. This article develops a dynamic model to examine a largely overlooked friction: Sharing power within an authoritarian regime bolsters the opposition's coercive capabilities. The resultant threat‐enhancing effect creates two distinct commitment problems for the opposition, which determine if and when power sharing occurs. First, the opposition cannot commit to refrain from leveraging its enhanced threat. The ruler prefers to incur a revolt than peacefully share power if the threat‐enhancing effect is large. Second, the threat‐enhancing effect tempts the opposition to wait for a future power‐sharing deal, which undercuts the opposition's commitment to revolt today. New dynamic implications arise: delayed power sharing, conflict, or an increased willingness for the ruler to share power are all possible. Scrutinizing the opposition's limited commitment ability contrasts with the predominant existing focus on the autocrat's commitment problem.

articles.title: Testing Hypotheses From the Social Approval Theory of Online Hate: An Analysis of 110 Million Messages From Parler
articles.authors: David M. Markowitz, Samuel Hardman Taylor
articles.abstract: We examined how social approval motivates online hate via the social approval theory, which argues social approval signals on hate messages predict (1) more hate speech, and (2) more toxicity. Using 110 million messages from Parler (2018–2021), we observed that upvotes on hate speech posts (messages broadcast on users’ profiles to followers’ feeds) predicted a lower probability of hate speech in the next immediate post but more in the following week’s posts. Additionally, upvotes on comments (messages embedded within conversational threads) negatively predicted hate speech in the next comment but positively predicted the degree of toxicity during the next week and month. Between-person effects revealed negative immediate short-term effects but positive longer-term effects for hate speech. For comments , social disapproval (downvotes) moderated these relationships, making them less positive at weekly through quarterly time-intervals and more strongly negative at 6-months. Social approval predicts online hate in time- and message-dependent ways.

articles.title: Do Political Conversations Persuade or Polarize? Evidence From a Real-Time Randomized Experiment
articles.abstract: Political conversations across lines of disagreement are central to democracy. While some individuals approach them as opportunities to learn, others treat them as battles to be won. Theory suggests these contrasting motivations may shape how individuals process information and respond to disagreement, yet their consequences for attitude dynamics during conversations remain unclear. We fill this gap through an experiment ( N = 466) that manipulates motivation in real-time video conversations between pairs of Israeli citizens holding opposing views on Israel–U.S. relations. We financially incentivized some participants to win the debate, others to learn their partner’s perspective, while a control group received no incentive. We find consistent evidence that a winning-oriented mindset reduces the likelihood of persuasion, while a learning-oriented mindset increases it. Notably, there is no evidence that motivation polarizes attitudes. Our findings suggest that a winning-oriented mindset undermines mutual understanding, whereas learning-based dialogue can help bridge political divides.

articles.title: Foreign Aid and Teenage Childbearing
articles.authors: Heather Congdon Fors, Dick Durevall, Ann‐Sofie Isaksson, Annika Lindskog
articles.abstract: Teenage childbearing has serious consequences for young mothers, their children, and society. This study estimates the impact of foreign aid projects on teenage fertility in Malawi. We combine georeferenced data on aid projects from 1998 to 2016 with individual‐level fertility data. Identification relies on spatial and temporal variation in aid exposure and survey timing, with controls for project placement and teenage childbearing among older women not exposed to the intervention. Results show that aid to sexual and reproductive health, HIV/AIDS, and education significantly reduce teenage fertility, while other aid types have limited effects. Women exposed to relevant aid during the critical age range were 11 percent less likely to have given birth as teenagers, with larger effects for women who were exposed for longer periods. The effect appears to operate mainly through increased school attendance and delayed marriage, but there is also some evidence for increased abstinence, contraceptive use, and family planning knowledge.

articles.title: Putting your money where your mouth is: Expressions of Chinese nationalist sentiments are not just cheap talk
articles.abstract: Do nationalist expressions reflect a willingness to pay costs or are they cheap talk? This is important because theories expect nationalism affects a wide range of outcomes that pose costs to participants, including international conflict and participation in boycotts. However, past research has either relied on self‐reports that cannot rule out cheap talk or outcome measures at higher levels of analysis, such as international trade flows, that do not directly link individual‐level nationalist sentiment to behavior. In contrast, we measure both nationalist sentiments and costly behavior on an individual level using the content of millions of Chinese social media posts and the nationality of the brand of users' devices, for example type of cellphone, as a costly behavioral measure. We find that nationalist sentiment makes citizens less likely to use US and Japanese brands with an instrumental variable analysis.

articles.title: Do “warm glow” feelings affect climate mitigation behaviors? A field experiment on consumer electric energy choices
articles.authors: Jennifer Jerit, Jason Barabas, Hwayong Shin, Molly Gahagen, Scott May
articles.abstract: Addressing the climate crisis is going to require behavioral change in many aspects of daily life. A growing literature suggests the promise of “warm glow” messaging that features the pleasure and satisfaction one experiences from acting sustainably. Yet previous research has relied almost exclusively on self‐reported behavioral intentions, leaving open whether such appeals meaningfully affect real‐world, costly choices. We partnered with a local organization to conduct a field experiment on energy choices in Hanover, New Hampshire. Using a randomized roll‐out design in early 2025, we systematically varied the timing of postcard mailers that contain a warm glow message encouraging customers to increase the renewable content of their energy option. Analyses of administrative data on consumer energy choices reveal that warm glow messages delivered in a field setting have a null effect on adoption of higher‐renewable power choices, with a small number of customers changing to the greener but more costly option. Our study provides novel behavioral evidence on the real‐world impact of intrinsic motivation appeals in the climate domain.

articles.title: Feeling the body politic: Interoception as a mechanism of political stress resilience
articles.abstract: Politics can substantially harm physical and mental health, especially in polarized contexts, making political polarization a major non‐medical cause of disease and suffering. We examined whether citizens can protect their health without undermining civic engagement. Across three studies with over 2000 participants during the 2022 U.S. midterms and 2024 presidential election, we show that interoceptive sensibility, that is, the ability to perceive and trust one's internal bodily signals, protects against politics' adverse health effects. Higher interoceptive sensibility consistently predicted lower emotional, physical, behavioral, and social health costs, controlling for political identity, demographics, and emotion regulation. During the charged 2024 election, it further predicted fewer negative emotions, more hope for the future, and less fear, particularly when their candidate lost. Interoceptive sensibility also correlated with political engagement and efficacy, suggesting it enhances rather than inhibits participation. Our findings highlight it as a promising trait for mitigating political stress without reducing civic involvement.

articles.title: Population Aging and Citizen Preferences for Automation and Immigration: A Cautionary Tale for Advanced Aging Economies?
articles.abstract: Extensive research highlights public apprehension toward immigrants and robots, but few studies examine how demographic challenges, particularly population aging, influence these perceptions. The public may not naturally consider population aging when evaluating immigration or automation policies, as these issues are often discussed in silos. We thus hypothesize that priming the public to consider population aging will lead them to view automation and immigration more favorably. Using pre‐registered survey experiments in three countries—Japan, South Korea, and France—we investigate whether providing factual information about population aging alters attitudes toward immigration and automation. We find that in Japan, the world's most aged country, such information generates more favorable attitudes toward both immigration and automation. In Korea, the fastest‐aging country, it improves only immigration attitudes. In France, where the elderly population is average for the EU, we find no significant effect. We find, however, that these positive effects in Japan and Korea do not persist when respondents consider automation and immigration policies alongside other options like adjusting the retirement age. These findings suggest that the public's policy preferences in response to population aging are subject to country‐specific contexts, as well as to different issue linkages activated in policy discussions.

articles.title: Lobbying Priorities in Agenda‐Setting: Agenda Breadth, Direction, and Responsiveness Across Economic and Citizen Groups
articles.abstract: Interest groups are key actors in shaping political agendas. Yet, we know surprisingly little about how they determine their lobbying priorities at the earliest stage of the policy process. This study advances a novel conceptual framework for studying interest groups' issue prioritization in the agenda setting stage along three complementary dimensions: agenda breadth, agenda direction, and agenda responsiveness. Drawing on original survey data from 630 EU level interest groups, our results show that issue prioritization is driven primarily by the type of constituents a group represents. Economic interest groups tend to pursue broader lobbying agendas, focus on defending the policy status quo, and are more responsive to internal member pressures when prioritizing undesired issues. Citizen groups, by contrast, typically adopt narrower agendas, prioritize challenging the status quo, and respond more strongly to external issue salience when determining their lobbying priorities. Overall, the study advances our understanding of how interest groups navigate competition for political attention and contributes to broader debates on agenda‐setting in contemporary democracies.
