articles.title: Beliefs About Public Opinion and the Perceived Legitimacy of Policy Decisions
articles.abstract: Democratic legitimacy is typically thought to depend on whether political decisions reflect public opinion, or majority preferences. Do citizens share this standard? And what if citizens are wrong about public opinion? We study how beliefs about public support for controversial policy proposals are associated with the perceived legitimacy of adopting them, and whether accurate polling information changes these judgments. In a representative survey experiment in Germany, respondents reported their own position on four such proposals, estimated public support, and rated the legitimacy of adopting each one. For a random subset of proposals, respondents received accurate polling information showing that the proposal lacked majority support. We find that perceived public support predicts legitimacy judgments even after accounting for respondents’ own policy preferences. Yet these perceptions are often inaccurate and shaped by respondents’ own views. Corrective polling information modestly lowers perceived legitimacy, especially among those who initially overestimated public support. The findings suggest that misperceptions of public opinion can distort, but accurate information can also partly correct, citizens’ assessments of democratic legitimacy.

articles.title: What Drives Voter Bias Against Muslim Politicians? An Experimental Examination
articles.abstract: Religious and ethnic minorities remain underrepresented in political office, but its reasons are debated. Using administrative data from Norwegian local elections, we show that candidates with Muslim names receive fewer personal votes, and propose that this is (partly) due to political beliefs about Muslims as politicians.To examine this claim, we identify salient political beliefs and implement a conjoint experiment that estimates anti-Muslim bias with and without information on these beliefs.In a low-information setting, respondents exhibit a substantial anti-Muslim bias, but providing belief-relevant information reduces this anti-Muslim bias by 2–5 percentage points. The largest reduction occurs when respondents learn candidates’ positions on minority-rights issues. This reduction is driven by right-wing voters and is large enough to eliminate the left-right gap in anti-Muslim bias. These findings show a strong political component in the anti-Muslim bias.

High-Skilled Migration Revisited: Foregrounding the Multinational Enterprise in Migration Infrastructures
articles.abstract: In this article, we extend migration-infrastructure scholarship by foregrounding multinational enterprises (MNEs) as structural actors that both co-produce high-skilled mobilities (direct effects) and reshape the broader conditions that render such mobilities feasible and attractive (indirect effects). On the direct side, we theorize three interlocking channels through which MNEs shape high-skilled migration: (1) recruiting, hiring, and relocating international talent; (2) generating organizationally mediated migration networks, shaped by senior corporate actors and enacted through international human resource management policies and practices; and (3) reinforcing the spatial concentration of global talent by strengthening clusters around global innovation and business hubs. These mechanisms are connected by a shared organizational logic—knowledge internalization—which links the three direct channels into a coherent account of firm-driven mobility. On the indirect side, MNEs influence the broader possibility space of high-skilled migration by reshaping political, economic, and sociocultural environments through corporate political strategies, global factory dynamics, and processes of forward and reverse diffusion. In this sense, MNEs may transform the contexts that, over time, orient and sustain subsequent high-skilled mobilities. Given their global reach and orchestration capacity, bringing MNEs more squarely into the analytical frame also matters beyond theory. It can inform policies better aligned with the organizational realities shaping contemporary migration.

Institutionalized negative selection and structural teacher favouritism: demystifying the effects of cultural capital on educational achievement in China
articles.abstract: Recent studies in China often report negative effects of cultural capital on educational achievement. This study revisits that claim by examining its effect, underlying mechanisms, and heterogeneity. Drawing on longitudinal data from the China Education Panel Survey, four main findings emerge. First, after accounting for negative selection, the supposed negative effects of cultural capital disappear. More broadly, cultural capital shows no significant overall effect on educational achievement, contrary to what cultural capital theory would usually predict. Nevertheless, cultural capital and educational achievement remain indirectly linked through institutional processes. Second, the analysis provides empirical support for a new concept, institutionalized negative selection, defined as a process in which low-achieving students select into extracurricular activities in pursuit of better educational credentials, a pattern supported by formal educational institutions. Third, although no evidence supports the conventional mechanisms that cultural capital reduces study time or enhances cognitive or non-cognitive learning skills, highbrow cultural participation is associated with greater structural teacher favouritism (i.e. praising and cold-calling on students in class), which in turn improves educational achievement. Fourth, institutionalized negative selection is found only among low-socioeconomic status (SES) students, supporting the cultural mobility model, whereas structural teacher favouritism is more pronounced among high-SES students and in high-SES schools, supporting the cultural reproduction model. These findings show that, in China, institutionalized negative selection and structural teacher favouritism are two important pathways linking cultural capital and educational achievement. This reveals how cultural capital can both promote educational mobility and perpetuate educational inequality, depending on how educational institutions value cultural capital.

articles.title: Is parents’ employment uncertainty linked to children's development? Analysing patterns and mechanisms in France
articles.authors: Marta Facchini, Lidia Panico, Carlo Barone
articles.abstract: Early childhood is a critical period for the reproduction of social inequality. While extant literature focuses on socio-economic background, less is known about the role of parents’ employment uncertainty, notwithstanding its significant presence in post-Fordist societies. We investigate the relationship between household employment uncertainty (HEU)—including temporary work and unemployment—and children's cognitive and socio-emotional development, as well as their physical health. We leverage four waves of the nationally representative French Longitudinal Study of Children (ELFE). First, using ordinary least squares and linear probability models, we find that the accumulation within the household and the persistence of HEU over time are both associated with lower cognitive development (up to −0.2 SD) at ages 2 and 3.5. Results for socio-emotional development are less robust, and physical health appears not to be correlated with HEU, possibly due to comprehensive healthcare. Second, we examine potential mechanisms using counterfactual mediation analysis. In line with the family investment and the family stress models, income and parental investment in cognitively-enhancing activities mediate the link with cognitive development, whereas parental stress mediates the association with socio-emotional development. Robustness tests include regression-with-residuals to account for other mediators and sibling birth as post-treatment confounders of the mediator–outcome link. Overall, HEU emerges as an important pathway in early inequality, calling for targeted policy.

Gender inclusivity and perceptions of party ideology: Observational and experimental evidence
articles.authors: James Adams, David Bracken, Noam Gidron, Will Horne, Seonghui Lee, Diana O’Brien, Lie Philip Santoso, Kaitlin Senk, Randolph T. Stevenson
articles.abstract: Do citizens use gender-based heuristics to infer political parties’ ideological positions? We posit that citizens view more ‘gender inclusive’ parties as more left-leaning than comparable male-dominated organizations. Cues about gender inclusivity, moreover, come not only from women’s presence in parties’ legislative delegations but also from other visible signals of women’s incorporation into parties – including as leaders and supporters – and through organizational rules promoting women’s inclusion. We present analyses of election survey data from 21 Western publics over time, which show that, controlling for the left–right tones of parties’ manifestos, citizens perceive more gender-inclusive parties as more left-wing and that the cumulative impact of the various dimensions of gender inclusivity is substantial. We next report experimental evidence from four countries, which provides further support for gender-based heuristics. Our findings highlight the importance of not just the message but also the messenger in shaping citizens’ assessments of parties’ ideological perceptions.

articles.title: Contested terrain: How attitudes toward gender issues relate to voting behavior
articles.abstract: While research increasingly links sexist attitudes to far-right support, public debates have moved well beyond women’s equality to encompass LGBTIQ+ rights. Yet studies have been slow to follow, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of attitudes toward trans, intersex, and non-binary people and how they associate with party choice, especially beyond far-right support. Drawing on original data from the German Social Cohesion Panel (2022/23), we are, to our knowledge, among the first to investigate a broader range of gender-related attitudes and find, first, that these constitute two empirically distinct dimensions, binary and non-heteronormative gender issues , that while conceptually intertwined, warrant separate examination. Second, while support for binary gender issues is widespread, non-heteronormative issues remain highly contested. Third, these dimensions relate differently to vote choice: attitudes toward binary gender issues show partisan sorting across the left-right spectrum, while attitudes toward non-heteronormative gender issues reveal a specific antagonism between the Greens and (center-)right parties. Finally, considering both dimensions together uncovers an asymmetry: voters of (center-)right parties form a cohesive conservative bloc, while supportive voters with different attitudinal profiles disperse across (center-)left parties.

articles.title: Legislators' Constituency Focus Across Electoral Systems
articles.abstract: Previous studies argue that incentives to cultivate a personal reputation and maximize personal votes make legislators more likely to focus on their constituencies in candidate‐centered than party‐centered systems. Empirical analyses, however, have yielded mixed support for this hypothesis. We provide new tests of the relationship between electoral system characteristics and constituency signaling in speeches, holding individual legislators fixed. We examine speeches given by legislators from England, Scotland, and Wales in the European Parliament (EP) and in the UK House of Commons. This allows us to follow the same legislators (1) across an electoral system change in the EP in 1999 and (2) when they move between the EP and the House of Commons. In line with expectations, we find that constituency signaling in speeches is more likely when the same legislators are elected under candidate‐centered rules.

Beyond the environmental burden narrative: environmental attitudes and green-job aspirations among Syrian refugees and Jordanians
articles.authors: Sijeong Lim, Hannah June Kim, Youcheer Kim, Youngwan Kim
articles.abstract: There is a prevalent view of refugees as an environmental burden, a narrative that can exacerbate strained relations between refugees and host communities. This study examines the empirical basis of this perspective using an original, in-person survey of 510 Syrian refugees and 509 Jordanian nationals across four cities in Jordan: Amman, Mafraq, Irbid, and Zarqa. The findings indicate that environmental attitudes and practices are broadly similar among Jordanians and Syrian refugees. Syrian refugees report modestly higher levels of environmental knowledge, a pattern that may reflect exposure to climate-related risks during war and displacement. In addition, Syrian refugees express greater interest in green jobs than Jordanians do, a pattern that may be associated with their disadvantaged position in the labor market and their search for new employment opportunities. These findings suggest that, under the right institutional design, refugees can contribute to the host nation’s green economy transition.

Generalizing Causal Effects with Noncompliance: Application to Deep Canvassing Experiments
articles.abstract: Standard approaches in generalizability often focus on generalizing the intent-to-treat effect. However, in practice, a more policy-relevant quantity is the generalized impact of an intervention across compliers. While instrumental variable methods are commonly used to estimate the complier average causal effect (CACE) within samples, standard approaches cannot be applied to a target population with a different distribution from the study sample. This article makes several key contributions. First, we introduce a new set of identifying assumptions in the form of a population-level exclusion restriction that allows for identification of the target CACE (T-CACE) in both randomized experiments and observational studies. This allows researchers to identify the T-CACE without relying on standard principal ignorability assumptions. Second, we propose a class of inverse-weighted estimators for the T-CACE and derive their asymptotic properties. We provide extensions for settings in which researchers have access to auxiliary compliance information across the target population. Finally, we introduce a sensitivity analysis for researchers to evaluate the robustness of the estimators in the presence of unmeasured confounding and extend existing tests to evaluate instrument validity in this context. We illustrate our proposed method through extensive simulations and a study evaluating the impact of deep canvassing on reducing exclusionary attitudes.

articles.title: Sick of change? Sickness absence following ownership conversions in Norwegian kindergartens
articles.authors: Håvard Thorsen Rydland, Dag Arne Christensen
articles.abstract: The expansion of mixed-provider welfare systems has intensified debates about the consequences of public, nonprofit, and for-profit provision. Existing research focuses primarily on efficiency, service quality, and citizens' outcomes, while less is known about ownership conversions’ consequences for employees. We depart from research suggesting that ownership conversions can disrupt employee-organization value congruence as well as change the incentive structures. Leveraging population-wide administrative data from Norwegian childcare services (2015-2019), we examine whether ownership conversions are associated with changes in employee sickness absence. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that sickness absence increases following nonprofit-to-for-profit conversions. At the same time, public-to-for-profit transitions show little consistent relationship with sickness absence. These findings suggest that employee responses to ownership change are shaped less by the public-private divide than by differences in organizational missions and values. More broadly, the study highlights organizational value congruence as a potential mechanism linking ownership arrangements to employee well-being, and suggests that the nonprofit-for-profit boundary may be more consequential for employees than the conventional public-private divide.

articles.title: Every Mile Counts: Geographical Distance as Administrative Burden in Intellectual Property Services
articles.abstract: While existing research has examined procedural and informational sources of administrative burden, this paper examines how organizational design choices about the geographic location of administrative authority institutionalize spatial burdens on firms. We leverage China's decentralization reform in trademark registration services as a natural experiment to test this theory. This reform reduced geographic distance by establishing local acceptance windows across the country from 2016 to 2019. Prior to this reform, trademark applications had to be submitted exclusively at the centralized Beijing office, imposing substantial geographic barriers on firms nationwide. Using a unique dataset covering over 37 million trademark applications from 294 Chinese cities, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences approach to estimate the causal effects of reduced geographic distance on trademark filings. We find that establishing local acceptance windows increased trademark applications by approximately 4.4 percent, or roughly 209,000 additional filings in 2019 alone. Moreover, the reform generated compound distributional outcomes: small and medium-sized enterprises responded more strongly than larger firms, and the new applicants drawn into the trademark system were concentrated in cities with thinner infrastructure. Mechanism analysis confirms that this increase is primarily driven by distance reduction rather than improvements in administrative efficiency or reductions in corruption. The findings provide large-scale causal evidence on the behavioral consequences of redistributing administrative service delivery across space, demonstrating that physical accessibility remains crucial for equitable service uptake even amid the digital transformation of administrative services.

Causal Attribution and Trust Evaluations in the Multilevel Structure of Civil-Military Relations
articles.abstract: Public trust in the military and the civilian leaders who control it is central to democratic governance and national security. However, we know relatively little about how such trust is formed. This study examines how citizens update their trust in each actor following military-related events and whether information about the multilevel structure fundamental to democratic civil-military relations influences this process. Existing research has largely relied on performance theories, which assume a straightforward causal link between event outcomes and trust, and on observational data that complicate causal identification. Building on attribution theory, this study refines performance-based accounts by highlighting the multilevel structure. It conducted three survey experiments and a supplementary survey in Japan, a consolidated democracy with a considerable armed force and a population with a relatively strict view on civilian control. The results indicate that event outcomes influence evaluations of civilian and military actors to a similar degree, although underlying mechanisms are asymmetrical depending on the outcome’s direction. Moreover, differing from theoretical expectations, information about the multilevel structure does not substantially alter the effect of outcome information on trust in most cases, although it shapes attributional reasoning. These findings challenge conventional understandings of trust and accountability in democratic civil-military relations.

articles.title: Beyond Incivility: Bellicose Politics, Violence, and the Dangers of Illiberal Encroachment in the United States
articles.abstract: The United States seems to be experiencing a volatile period where its core values and institutions have come under threat, accompanied by what many observers identify as a rise in uncivil speech and behavior. Yet, much of this contentious rhetoric and behavior seemingly goes beyond instances of incivility and into something more serious, including threats, intimidation, physical assaults, insurrectionary riots, and assassination. This raises two important questions: is the concept of incivility adequate for describing and analyzing such speech and behavior in contemporary politics, and how should threats and violent actions be understood within a broader civility framework? In this article, I argue that many of the illiberal pathologies afflicting contemporary democracies—including political violence—fall outside the scope of incivility. Drawing on recent work in normative political theory, I unpack the concept of civility and examine how violent speech and actions fit within its various dimensions. I then introduce the concept of “bellicose politics” and provide examples from the United States in which contentious rhetoric and behavior exceed the bounds of incivility. I conclude by considering how this concept may improve the way we analyze and respond to violent rhetoric and actions in political life.

articles.title: An Analysis of Position-Taking and Position-Avoidance in the U.S. House of Representatives
articles.authors: Jason S. Byers, Laine P. Shay
articles.abstract: Scholars of legislative politics have extensively explored the political factors that incentivize members of Congress to engage in position-taking. This has led to a well-developed body of work focusing on why legislators skip congressional roll-call votes. Current scholarship offers mixed conclusions on whether electoral considerations influence a representative’s likelihood of abstaining from a roll-call vote. To help clarify these mixed findings, we analyze a broader range of electoral forces. In this study, we examine all roll-call abstentions among members serving in the U.S. House of Representatives from the 85th to the 117th Congress. We find that electoral considerations can indeed impact abstention behavior; however, the effect depends on the type of election. Specifically, lawmakers vulnerable in their primary race are more likely to avoid taking a position on a roll-call vote, whereas electoral vulnerability in the general election appears to have little effect. These findings deepen our understanding of how elections influence representation.

Losing the engaged without winning the disengaged: Personalism and the choice of political news
articles.abstract: When political news centers on the policy work or private lives of individual politicians rather than on parties, it can obscure the collective actors citizens must judge at elections. The usual defense is that such personalism attracts readers, especially those otherwise unlikely to choose political news. We test this claim in survey experiments in Denmark, the United Kingdom, and the United States ( N = 3039). Respondents chose between an entertainment article and a political article whose subheadline attributed a new bill to a party, an individual politician (individualized), or the politician’s personal story (privatized). Personalism recruited no readers. Effects are negative in all countries and pooled amount to a significant five percentage point loss. The losses were concentrated among politically engaged citizens, while the least engaged, the very readers personalism is meant to attract, were unmoved. Party-centered news thus entail no audience sacrifice as citizens prefer the format that keeps parties visible.

articles.title: Is sidestepping the judiciary seen as democratic? Evidence from Great Britain and Spain
articles.authors: Noam Titelman, Javier Sajuria, Lisa Zanotti
articles.abstract: Executives often bypass the courts without public backlash and, sometimes, with public support. This research note evaluates one strategy employed by politicians for securing public backing when bypassing the courts: a majoritarian framing. We evaluate this strategy through candidate survey experiments in Great Britain ( n = 957) and Spain ( n = 995) that contrast this framing with institutional checks and balances. On average, respondents rate the candidate pushing for court bypassing as less democratic. Nevertheless, a sizeable minority in both countries judges this option as more democratic. These results indicate that heterogeneous understandings of what counts as democratic can sustain public tolerance for executive bypass of the courts.

Estimation of Latent Group Structures in Time-Varying Panel Data Models
articles.authors: Paul Haimerl, Stephan Smeekes, Ines Wilms
articles.abstract: We consider panel data models where coefficients change smoothly over time and follow a latent group structure, being homogeneous within but heterogeneous across groups. To jointly estimate the group memberships and group-specific coefficient trajectories, we propose FUSE-TIME, a pairwise adaptive group fused-Lasso estimator combined with polynomial spline sieves. We establish consistency, derive the asymptotic distributions of the penalized sieve estimator and its post-selection version, and show oracle efficiency. Monte Carlo experiments demonstrate strong finite-sample performance in terms of estimation accuracy and group identification. An application to the CO2 intensity of GDP highlights the relevance of addressing both cross-sectional heterogeneity and time-variance in empirical exercises within climate econometrics.

Practicing love with algorithms: How online communities narrate and make sense of human–AI intimacy
articles.authors: Fanjue Liu, Haiyan Hao, Kun Xu
articles.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in everyday life, emotionally intimate interactions with AI companions are becoming increasingly visible. Yet prior research has focused mainly on individual experiences, leaving limited understanding of how human–AI intimacy is collectively interpreted and negotiated in online communities. This study examines community discourse on RedNote, a major Chinese social and lifestyle platform, using 13,059 comments from 58 relevant posts. Combining BERTopic modeling with a human–large language model (LLM) hybrid emotion classification procedure, the analysis identifies three thematic clusters: intimacy as co-construction, intimacy as infrastructure, and intimacy as boundary negotiation. Co-construction centers on persona design, roleplay, and narrative world-building and is marked mainly by joy and curiosity. Infrastructure-related discourse is associated with frustration and sadness, while boundary negotiation reflects ambivalence toward intimacy with AI.

articles.title: Haste makes waste: How public pressure increases legislative duration in the European Union
articles.authors: Anastasia Ershova, Aleksandra Khokhlova, Nikoleta Yordanova
articles.abstract: While increased decision-making complexity and membership predispose the European Union to protracted negotiations and legislative gridlock, still some legislative proposals are adopted faster than others. What explains this variation? Drawing on models of democratic responsiveness, we argue that politicisation potential – captured by public salience, opinion division, and planned European Union authority expansion – increases legislative duration. To test our expectations, we measure public opinion using Eurobarometer surveys and classify the integration potential of legislative proposals between 2009 and 2019 using semi-supervised machine learning. Our findings indicate that European Union policymakers legislate longer on policies of higher public salience and proposals broadening the European Union authority. These results contribute to research on policymaking responsiveness and efficiency in supranational settings, demonstrating how politicisation affects legislative processes in the European Union.

articles.title: Civil resistance in the climate age: generational agency and the new grammar of protest
Protestantism and insurance—an elective affinity? A multilevel comparative-historical analysis of the confessional insurance gap
articles.abstract: While there are many studies and theories about the rise of social insurance and the public welfare state, the prior emergence and growth of private life and nonlife insurance are largely understudied, mostly due to a lack of data. This article fills this gap by testing whether there is an elective affinity between the rise and evolution of private insurance and Protestantism that is irreducible to typical factors external to religion (gross domestic product, education, demography, public welfare). Drawing on multiple new datasets, the paper tests whether Catholic–Protestant differences in insurance demand persist when controlling for standard covariates external to religion across nineteen OECD countries (1870–2020), across states in the confessionally mixed federations of Germany, Switzerland and the USA (1876–2020) as well as across US counties and European cities around 1909. The article finds Lutheran and Reformed Protestant areas to have had higher private insurance penetration and density than Catholic ones, controlling for standard covariates. This relationship is more pronounced in life than nonlife branches, more pronounced for insurance demand than insurance company activity, and more consistently found in Europe than within the USA. More generally, the article suggests that the confessional insurance gap may provide a missing empirical link to better understand the emergence of Alpine and Maritime insurance cultures, different premodern poor-ethics traditions and the different worlds of modern welfare states and pension systems.

Discrimination in Bureaucratic Recruitment Under Civil Service Exams
articles.abstract: Meritocratic recruitment is a central tenet in Weber's theory of bureaucracy, which states that employees should be hired based on merit. However, extensive research has shown evidence of hiring discrimination against minorities, breaking with basic principles in bureaucratic selection. This paper examines whether ethnic and racial minorities are discriminated against when bureaucratic organizations use civil service exams to assess candidates' merit and fitness for positions. Drawing on data from the local government of New York City and a candidate list fixed effects approach, we find that Black and Hispanic candidates are slightly more likely to be hired than White candidates with similar exam scores, suggesting that these ethnic minorities hold a small advantage in bureaucratic selection. However, examining the starting compensation levels of new hires, we show that minorities are hired at lower salaries and are compensated less for high exam scores than comparable White hires. Our findings suggest that civil service exams might be an important lever for securing fair and unbiased bureaucratic selection but also that they do not prevent discrimination in later steps of the recruitment process.

articles.title: The Co-optation of Civil Society: How International Organizations Manage Contention
articles.abstract: How do international organizations manage social discontent while opening their governance processes to civic actors? This essay conceptualizes co-optation as a mode of contention management through which international institutions selectively integrate critical voices into participatory arrangements that channel, moderate, and reframe dissent in more regulated forms of engagement. Moving beyond rationalist accounts that treat co-optation as a strategic exchange between rulers and challengers, the article develops a relational framework attentive to sustained interactions among bureaucratic agents, civic actors, experts, and intermediaries. It argues that co-optation operates through institutional infrastructures and cross-boundary chains that stabilize cooperation, organize access, socialize civic actors, and expose critical claims to filtering and normative alignment. These chains do not eliminate the agency of co-opted actors. Rather, they make agency part of the process through which critique becomes institutionally acceptable. The article contributes to international studies by showing how international organizations manage contention through relational forms of capture, and how advocacy engagement can help stabilize institutional authority.

articles.title: Ontological Security Research in International Politics: Assessing the Evolution of a Research Tradition
articles.abstract: Ontological security has become one of the most dynamic and theoretically rich bodies of scholarship in International Relations (IR), guiding research across levels of analysis and diverse domains of world politics. Given its flexibility, inclusiveness, and epistemological and methodological plurality, however, scholars have raised questions about its coherence and analytical distinctiveness. Existing reviews have thoughtfully mapped its richness and scope, but they have been less able to address a central puzzle: How can ontological security research remain theoretically coherent while becoming increasingly plural? This article addresses this puzzle by drawing on Larry Laudan’s philosophy of science. It explains why Laudan’s framework, rather than the more familiar alternatives—Kuhnian paradigms and Lakatosian research programmes—is better suited to capturing this kind of plural scholarly formation. It argues that ontological security scholarship is best understood as a developing research tradition and theory complex: an open and plural formation that connects different theoretical strands, remains anchored in a relatively stable conceptual core, and evolves through empirical and conceptual problem-solving. Viewed through this lens, the plurality of ontological security research should not be read as fragmentation, but as evidence of a productive research tradition whose development depends on synthesizing theories, integrating concepts, and opening new analytical pathways. The article shows that ontological security scholarship contributes to IR by generating alternative accounts of empirical phenomena, connecting levels of analysis, and bridging epistemological approaches. By tracing this development, the article demonstrates why ontological security research remains coherent despite its diversity and how it equips scholars with conceptual tools to pose and address significant questions in world politics. In doing so, it highlights both the overlooked relevance of Laudan’s framework to IR and the broader disciplinary contribution of ontological security research.

articles.title: Rebuilding Trust in Higher Education: Strategies for Addressing the “Diploma Divide”
articles.abstract: The Trump administration is using all the levers of executive power to intervene in universities, including multimillion-dollar cuts, investigations into federal regulation violations, visa withdrawals for international students, and ideological pressures. The outcome of this fight over the purpose of higher education could shape the sector for decades. This reflection essay argues that these attacks have been facilitated by a decade-long loss of public trust in higher education. It addresses two main questions: Why have colleges and universities lost the support of society, and what should they do to restore public trust? The essay argues that this loss of support is driven primarily by rising costs, perceived ideological bias, and questions about degree value. By situating these discussions within scholarship on polarization, populist backlash, and the “diploma divide,” this essay moves beyond causes to explore sector-specific solutions. These include improving educational access, redefining political messaging, demonstrating nonpartisanship, supporting their communities, redefining diversity to include social class, and bridging the cultural divide to protect the university as a democratic institution.

articles.title: Possessive Familialism and the Crisis of Democracy in the United States
articles.abstract: Amid rising concern over a crisis of democracy in the United States, one point of political alignment across the political spectrum stands out: valorization of the family. This is especially striking because it would seem to conflict with the core ethos of the dominant neoliberal political rationality. We propose that both convergence and crisis are fueled by a logic of possessive familialism. Taking up recent feminist, Marxist, and critical analyses of neoliberalism to situate our claim and tracing the genealogy of this thinking to John Locke, we argue that possessive familialism more aptly describes foundational commitments and assumptions of liberal, and now neoliberal, politics. At the core of the governing rationality of our time, the solo, self-sufficient family obscures the realities of human interdependence and fuels capitalist extraction and accumulation. Feeding the fantasy that individuals, families, and polities survive—and even thrive—absent cross-cutting, overlapping nests of social supports, possessive familialism is the linchpin of neoliberal political rationality that starves democratic imagination, culture, and structures, and fuels the current crisis. We identify five elements of possessive familialism; illustrate its operations through several contemporary examples, including the case for marriage equality and the COVID-19 pandemic; and show how it threatens the very conditions of democratic politics in the US.

articles.title: Salinization and Development,
articles.abstract: Climate change-intensified seawater intrusion creates a dual shock of transitory freshwater shortages and lasting soil degradation. We study its impacts on agricultural production in the Vietnamese Mekong Delta, a major rice exporter. Combining river salinity observations and detailed canal network data to map localized hydrological shocks, we find that salinity reduces rice yields but generates disproportionately larger declines in output and revenue. These losses are driven by a contraction in land under cultivation and limited substitution toward salt-resistant crops, pointing to constrained short-run adaptation. Using household and firm data, we further document reductions in own-farm employment alongside minimal transition to non-agricultural sectors, suggesting frictions in labor adjustment. Beyond income effects predicted by Engel curves, households reallocate expenditures toward healthcare and children’s schooling. The increase in schooling spending is driven by higher participation and may reflect shifts in opportunity costs, though we cannot rule out forward-looking responses.

articles.title: Matching on Gender and Sexual Orientation,
articles.abstract: We study the mating patterns of non-heterosexual individuals, who represent a significant and increasing portion of the population, particularly among the youth. We estimate a multidimensional matching model of the marriage market where partner’s gender is endogenously chosen conditional on the agent’s sexual orientation, and is subject to trade-offs that depend on both the agents’ preferences and the pool of potential partners. We show that same-sex couples experience lower gains from live-in relationships, a “same-sex penalty”. Absent this penalty, the share of same-sex couples in the U.S. would increase by about 50% (from 1.36% to 2.04% of all couples).

articles.title: A Dual Perspective on Community Mobility: Home‐Centric Place Networks and Older Adults' Mental Health in Shanghai During the Pandemic
articles.authors: Felicia F. Tian, Lei Xin, Mengying Zhou, Yuhan You, Chen Yang, Yang Chen
articles.abstract: Older adults' community mobility reflects both spatial and relational aspects of aging in place within urban environments. To capture this duality, we introduce a home‐centric place network framework that links the home to community destinations older adults routinely visit. The spatial dimension is measured using standard movement metrics, while the relational dimension is defined as opportunities for social encounters (sociability) and operationalized as the overlap of neighbors' routine activities across community places. We tested this framework by collecting two waves of GIS‐based mobility data and an online survey from 64 community‐dwelling older adults in Shanghai, a rapidly aging megacity, during the COVID‐19 pandemic. Results showed that older adults' place networks were diverse, but both the frequency of out‐of‐home visits and sociability declined sharply following a major outbreak. Those who were more mobile and sociable before the outbreak experienced greater reductions, and sociability was associated with more negative expectations. As social places became associated with higher infection risk, the pandemic fundamentally altered the relational meaning of community mobility. Overall, our findings demonstrate that a home‐centric place network framework deepens population geography by linking physical mobility, social encounters, and the emotional well‐being of older adults.

articles.title: Afghan as (Racialized) “Other”: Politics of Farsi Academic Knowledge Production on Migration in Iran
articles.abstract: This article critically investigates the politics of academic knowledge production on Afghan migration in Iran, posing the question: how does Iranian academia contribute to bordering strategies that marginalize Afghans? Drawing on a qualitative thematic analysis of 114 Farsi academic articles from the Iranian National Library's database—the point at which thematic saturation was reached within an initial corpus of 210 retrieved by keyword search—this study reveals how scholarly discourses construct Afghans as a racialized and securitized “other.” The analysis identifies five recurring themes: (1) measuring security, (2) measuring difference, (3) the pathology of presence, (4) measuring attitudes, and (5) racism and knowledge production on migration. These thematic findings illustrate how Iranian academic discourse problematizes migration, treating it as a deviation that justifies exclusionary practices. By pathologizing and racializing migration, academic narratives align with state‐driven bordering strategies that dehumanize vulnerable populations and normalize systemic inequalities. The study critiques the ethical failures of such exclusionary knowledge production, emphasizing its role in legitimizing state control and reinforcing public hostility toward marginalized groups. By connecting these findings to global debates on migration and the ethics of knowledge production, this work calls for a reflexive approach to studying migration, one that challenges the systemic injustices perpetuated by exclusionary discourses.

articles.title: Migration and the Geography of Life Expectancy: Selective Sorting and Spatial Dependence Across 172 Countries
articles.abstract: International migration has grown rapidly in recent decades, yet its relationship with population health is difficult to disentangle from the economic, structural and geographic characteristics of the places migrants move to. This study examines whether international migration is associated with population‐level life expectancy after accounting for confounding and the data's spatial structure. Data for 172 countries (189 in the spatial analyses) for 1990–2024 were assembled, combining migrant stock statistics from UN DESA, life expectancy estimates from Gapminder, and economic indicators from the World Bank. The analysis used cross‐sectional and panel data methods (pooled Ordinary Least Squares, country fixed effects, and first differences), spatial lag and spatial error models, spatial panel models, multiscale geographically weighted regression (MGWR), and an origin–destination analysis of bilateral migrant stocks. Migration and life expectancy were positively associated across countries (r = 0.42, p < 0.001), but the cross‐sectional migration coefficient was reduced by 47% after adjustment for GDP per capita, and no association was detectable within countries over time (fixed effects β = −0.13, p = 0.051; first differences β = −0.04, p = 0.744). Life expectancy was strongly spatially clustered (Moran's I = 0.68), and migration showed no detectable association with life expectancy once spatial dependence was modelled. MGWR indicated that the migration–life expectancy relationship was effectively global in scale and non‐significant, whereas unexplained place effects varied at a sub‐continental scale. Eighty percent of international migrants lived in a country with higher life expectancy than their country of origin. These findings suggest that the cross‐national association reflects the selective sorting of migrants towards already healthier places, compounded by spatial dependence, rather than an independent effect of migration on population health. More broadly, they extend the selective‐sorting framework from the subnational to the international scale and highlight the importance of geographic structure in interpreting migration–health relationships.

articles.title: Moral Narratives, Fragile Rights and Educational Striving Among Floating Lives in Urban Vietnam
articles.authors: Nguyen Hoang Thien, Nguyen Hoang Yen
articles.abstract: This study examines how Vietnamese returnees from Cambodia living on houseboats along a canal in urban Vietnam experience residence and citizenship in everyday life. Water‐based dwelling and cross‐border migration histories combine to produce a grey space in which residents are neither fully recognised nor consistently removed, despite holding Vietnamese nationality. Living on waterways outside planning compliance places households beyond the administrative categories used to distribute welfare, healthcare and residency verification, producing differentiated citizenship in practice. Residents respond through what the study terms moral infrastructure: hardship narratives, accounts of a life that burdens no one, and caregiving responsibilities used as practical grounds for negotiating tolerance with authorities. They also rely on manual work and relationships with ‘quý nhân’ and ‘mạnh thường quân’ (benevolent doctors, donors and volunteers) to meet everyday needs. Education, meanwhile, serves as a future‐oriented strategy through which families hope the next generation will gain the security and recognition they lack. Theoretically, the study extends Yiftachel's grey space framework beyond land‐based contexts and develops Holston's differentiated citizenship by showing that access to welfare depends on residency registration rather than nationality. It also proposes moral infrastructure as a complement to Simone's people‐as‐infrastructure. Practically, it calls for welfare eligibility to be decoupled from residency documentation, governance to be made more consistent and less discretionary and population frameworks to ensure that cross‐border return histories are not treated as a basis for administrative suspicion or unequal treatment.

articles.title: Temporal Access and Gendered Care: Livelihoods, Staying and Migration in Vietnam's Coastal Mangrove Communities
articles.authors: Ly Quoc Dang, Huynh Van Da, K. David Harrison, Mai Phuc Thinh
articles.abstract: Access to coastal resources depends not only on property, governance and proximity but also on whether ecological, household and bodily demands can be coordinated. This article examines how Khmer women negotiate mangrove and marine livelihoods in three coastal phum (villages) in Sóc Trăng, Vietnam's Mekong Delta. Drawing on an ethnographic case study, 13 narrative interviews (7 conducted as mobile interviews), participant observation and informal conversations, it examines temporal access, productive–reproductive coordination and staying or migration. Access depended on aligning tides, weather, routes, transport, bodily capacity, care and market waiting. Childcare, illness, cultivation and ritual obligations shaped whether and when livelihood work could occur. Women's local availability often sustained households while others migrated, although care could also organise collective movement. The article develops chronotopic care to explain this gendered coordination and cautions against equating livelihood continuity with resilience.

articles.title: Reworking Im/Mobility Scripts Across Generations: Leaving, Staying and Returning in Rural Taiwan
articles.abstract: Recent research on rural im/mobility has shown that leaving, staying and returning are meaningful life‐course processes rather than residual outcomes of migration. Building on this discussion, this article develops the concept of rural im/mobility scripts to examine the normative mobility pathways and meanings attached to leaving, staying and returning. These scripts are historically and spatially constituted, but are also reworked through biographical experience as conditions change. Drawing on life‐history interviews with 28 rural returnees and stayers in Yunlin and Chiayi, Taiwan, most born between 1971 and 1990, the analysis identifies 3 interrelated processes across the life course. First, during adolescence, participants inherited a taken‐for‐granted outmigration script in which leaving was highly institutionalised through educational expansion, parental expectations, urban success imaginaries and the devaluation of rural work, yet often weakly planned in practice. Second, in adulthood, they re‐legitimated staying and returning through locally grounded mobility, using transport, commuting, digital platforms, cross‐place markets and skills acquired elsewhere to build adequate lives and pursue local achievement from their hometowns. Third, as parents, they translated their own im/mobility experiences into a conditional expectation of self‐directed mobility for the next generation: children should know their hometown, see the world and ultimately decide whether to leave, stay and return. Following one generation from youth into parenthood, this article shows that rural im/mobility scripts are revised across the life course and translated into expectations for the next generation.

articles.title: Home in Motion: Eritrean Diasporic Experiences and the Negotiation of Home Across Transnational Spaces
articles.abstract: This article examines how unequal legal, economic, and mobility conditions shape homemaking among Eritrea's contemporary ‘generation of asylum.’ Drawing on 160 survey responses and 13 in‐depth interviews, it compares Eritreans living in first‐asylum settings in Uganda and Ethiopia, categorised as OAUE, with those living in European destination settings in Italy and Sweden, categorised as OEUIS. The findings show that political estrangement from the Eritrean state can coexist with enduring affective attachment to Eritrea, while participants’ capacities to establish home in their countries of residence vary substantially. The comparison identifies a ‘proximity paradox’: participants living geographically closer to Eritrea in OAUE may experience weaker host‐country belonging than those living farther away in OEUIS because of greater legal insecurity, restricted mobility, and constrained economic opportunities. These inequalities can also stratify transnational homemaking. Regional cities, weddings and family reunions can provide temporary homing through cultural continuity and familial connection, but access to these spaces is unevenly enabled by travel documentation and economic security. Aspirations for return are similarly conditional on political and legal change rather than expressions of nostalgia alone. The article contributes to migration and diaspora scholarship by conceptualising temporary homing as a provisional and unequally accessible process shaped by migrants’ positions within unequal mobility regimes.

articles.title: Trading migration? Explaining mobility provisions in preferential trade agreements
articles.authors: Philipp Lutz, Sandra Lavenex, Paula Hoffmeyer-Zlotnik
articles.abstract: Notwithstanding a generally unfavorable political climate regarding international migration, preferential trade agreements (PTAs) increasingly include provisions facilitating the temporary movement of specific categories of workers. Today, approximately seven in ten newly concluded PTAs contain clauses that enable the mobility of workers and businesspeople—particularly business visitors and intra-corporate transferees, who constitute a substantial share of skilled temporary migration in advanced industrial economies. This trend is striking given states’ longstanding emphasis on preserving sovereign control over migration policy. This article investigates the drivers of mobility provisions in PTAs and the implications for broader economic and migration policy. We develop and test three theoretical logics: (1) a trade logic grounded in interests resulting from economic interdependence; (2) a politics logic centered on migration control objectives; and (3) an institutional logic emphasizing path dependence and diffusion. Drawing on the MITA dataset, which codes mobility provisions in PTAs globally from 1960 to 2020, we find that economic interdependence and institutional path dependence are the primary forces behind mobility provisions, while migration control prerogatives have little explanatory power for either the presence, scope, or depth of these provisions. Our findings underscore the economic rationale behind mobility provisions in trade agreements, highlighting a pattern of selective liberalization for highly skilled workers and an increasingly fragmented landscape of migration governance.

articles.title: Stefano Recchia. 2025. Strategies for Approval: Building Support for Military Intervention at the UN Security Council. (New Haven: Yale University Press)
Same Race, Different Paths: Socialization, Orientation, and the Black Partisan Gender Gap
articles.abstract: Black women have long anchored Black political cohesion, yet little explains why a gender gap persists within a group marked by strong Democratic loyalty. Drawing on historical and sociological work, we argue that Black women’s collective-first orientation—shaped by gendered social roles across enslavement, Jim Crow, and modern civic life—heightens the political significance of the antecedents of Black Democratic partisanship: racial identity salience, perceived discrimination, and racially homogenous social networks. Using an original national survey of 4,200 Black Americans, we find that the partisan gender gap widens because the composition of their social networks more strongly shapes Black women’s political preferences. Accounting for racial identity salience and perceived discrimination substantially reduces the gender gap. These findings illuminate how racialized gender roles structure the pathways through which group-based norms translate into partisan behavior, providing a mechanism for intragroup variation and guiding more nuanced strategies for political engagement and mobilization.

articles.title: Testifying in Texas: Reflecting on We Testify Texas , a State-based Abortion Storyteller Retreat
articles.abstract: “I want to talk about my complicated feelings and how I was treated during my abortion procedure,” a Texas 20-something declared as they 1 hoisted themself out of the pool’s deep end. Three others considered the proposed topic and quickly tiptoed across the surrounding hot deck toward the shaded chairs to join the conversation. The 22 Texans lounging around the pool deck were part of We Testify ’s first state-based abortion storytelling cohort, We Testify Texas , held at a small retreat center in Mineola, a rural town east of Dallas in 2019. The We Testify Texas program sought to strengthen the state’s robust reproductive justice organizational advocacy infrastructure by training Texans who have had abortions 2 to share their stories and engage with advocacy efforts to preserve and expand abortion access and challenge hostile criminalization efforts in Texas. Although storytelling has been a tactic integral to feminist and social justice organizing (Fernandes 2017; Ganz 2024; Polletta 2022; Ross 2008), nonprofit organizational efforts primarily focused on the production of stories for public consumption, rather than engagement with the storytellers as local experts and organizers. This creates a transactional relationship between advocacy organizations and the people most impacted by the issue, separating storytellers from their stories and leaving storytellers as an untapped resource of testimonial expertise in communities. How can social justice movements and advocacy organizations center people who have had abortion experiences to lead cultural and state-based policy change work? This Notes from the Field reflects on the We Testify storytelling model as implemented through the We Testify Texas program, including the national-local partnership, programmatic activities, impact of the cohort, and how such a program could be replicated in similar political climates and distinct communities.

articles.title: Tragic but Rare: Abortion Storytelling in Local News Coverage One Year Past-Dobbs
articles.abstract: This essay examines local news coverage of abortion stories during the year following the United States Supreme Court decision, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022), in states with trigger bans and states considering legislation to severely restrict abortion. Framing theory stipulates that news narratives are never neutral. The way stories are structured inevitably foregrounds certain themes while pushing others to the margins (Chong and Druckman 2007; Pope, Pelletier, and Guertin 2018). We analyzed 1600 local news articles 1 for the presence of thematic frames, which focus on the big-picture context of a political event, and episodic frames, which more closely resemble a case study (Feezell, Glazier, and Boydstun 2021; Iyengar 1994). Our initial framing analysis found that only a small handful of articles, 66 out of 1,600, used episodic frames to tell the abortion stories of individuals. 2

articles.title: Why Activist Stories Matter and How They Lead to Change: The Reproductive Privacy Act in Rhode Island
articles.authors: Jordan Banick, Mikaila Mariel Lemonik Arthur
articles.abstract: “ Roe v. Wade is not going to be overturned. I think that’s a concern that’s not founded in reality,” said Rhode Island House Speaker Nicholas Mattiello in 2018 (Donnis 2022). As much as his words stung activists working to protect the right to abortion, they also signaled that he was out of touch with concerns about access to abortion in the nation as well as the state. National polling generally shows that 7 in 10 people support the right to abortion, and the same was true in Rhode Island (Bender 2018). So how did the smallest, most Catholic state in the United States manage to legislatively protect the right to abortion in 2019 without his support or the support of Rhode Island Senate Leadership?

articles.title: Climate, Nature, and the Uneven Expansion of Financial Governance
articles.abstract: Financial authorities have developed extensive climate‐related policies, but nature‐related financial policy remains less widespread. Using data on individual policy instruments across 116 jurisdictions from 2000 to 2025, this paper compares the adoption, policy areas, binding status, and source of climate‐ and nature‐related policies. Nature‐related policies appear in 27 jurisdictions, compared with 60 for climate‐only policies. National nature adoption is positively associated with a larger existing body of climate and environmental financial policies, mainly through the broader environmental component rather than climate‐specific policy. Climate‐only policies are used more frequently in prudential supervision and credit allocation than policies that combine nature with climate or broader environmental concerns. Nature‐related policies have a higher mandatory share over the full period but a lower share than climate‐only policies in 2023–2025. In the European Union, broad EU‐level coverage coexists with limited national issuance. The paper contributes a common framework for comparing climate and nature policies and distinguishes EU‐level coverage from national policy development. The results show that the climate‐nature gap concerns not only adoption, but also where policies are used, how binding they are, and which level of authority issues them.

articles.title: How the European Union Fell Out of Love With Open‐Source Software
articles.abstract: This article explains why the European Commission diluted the 2004 European Interoperability Framework's provisions favoring open‐source software and open standards when it revised the framework in 2010. Using an extended Multiple Streams Framework with a technology stream, the study shows how pro‐openness policy entrepreneurs secured the 2004 provisions and why incumbent advocacy became more effective during revision. Drawing on annotated drafts and expert interviews, the study traces actors' lobbying strategies across the problem, politics, and policy streams and examines how technology‐stream developments altered the feasibility and political salience of competing solutions. The analysis shows how changing standards and licensing dynamics, incumbent advocacy, and declining political support for the earlier pro‐openness package enabled a new coupling around business‐model neutrality and licensing flexibility, diluting the 2004 provisions. Beyond the European case, the study informs debates on open‐source artificial intelligence and advances theory on institutional dynamics in regulatory governance.

articles.title: Form Before Capability? AI Governance Adoption, Functional Capability, and the Limits of Index‐Based Evidence in the Global South
articles.abstract: Governments across the developing world have adopted artificial intelligence governance instruments at high speed, though the relationship between formal adoption and the capability to operate those instruments remains poorly understood. This article asks whether the expansion of AI governance architecture across the Global South has been matched by the functional capabilities on which regulatory effectiveness depends, and what explains the answer. Drawing on panel data for 82 countries across five Global South regions and six waves of the Government AI Readiness Index, it reports that within the period of stable index architecture (2020–2024) measures of regulatory form rose by 20.3 points on a 0–100 scale while measures of functional capability rose by 0.4 points, a within‐country differential present in 90% of sample countries and surviving removal of the single step‐scored indicator of national strategy adoption. The pattern of the differential discriminates among explanations: formal adoption rose four times faster in states in the top quartile of administrative capacity than in the bottom quartile, where capability fell; the most aid‐dependent states adopted least; and the differential is unrelated to regime type. This is inconsistent with the view that legislation is simply quicker to produce than infrastructure and with the view that adoption is decoupled from performance for external audiences, and consistent with adoption conditioned on administrative capacity, in which capability in the weakest states erodes while capability in stronger states grows more slowly than the instruments that depend on it. Vietnam and India are developed as confirming and deviant cases. Cross‐national dispersion widened on both dimensions, and patterns that appear only when the 2025 wave is included cannot be separated from the redesign of the index in that year.

Collective intentionality in international relations: a reductionist view
articles.abstract: The concept of collective intentionality has come to play an increasingly prominent role in the theoretical study of international relations (IR). In particular, scholars regularly treat two kinds of collectives – states and groups of states – as forming intentions and engaging in the joint pursuit of shared goals. In this piece, we intervene in the burgeoning IR debate on the ontology underlying this practice by making the case for a reductionist view of state intentions and joint interstate action. Drawing on Michael Bratman’s work on social ontology and original supporting arguments, we develop a sophisticated, non-summative reductionist account which overcomes many of the theoretical concerns that previously led scholars to reject reductionism as a viable ontological view within IR. Our account promises to advance both the empirical and normative study of international politics in several ways: it entails guidelines on how to study the origins of foreign policies and grand strategies; it lays the groundwork for novel views on interstate cooperation as it takes place in formats such as coalitions of the willing or security concerts; and it provides a promising framework for assessing collective moral responsibility and its relation to individual responsibility.
