articles.title: Deceit between Falshoods and Morality: Unpacking Audience Engagement with Disinformation
articles.authors: Sabina Mihelj, Stefan Janjić, Hanna Orsolya Vincze, Andreea Alina Mogoş
articles.abstract: Disinformation is customarily approached through an epistemic lens and defined with reference to intentionally false or misleading information. Yet, this approach struggles to account for how disinformation functions as a communicative practice that acquires meaning through audience interpretation and interaction. To develop a more comprehensive understanding, we draw on the analysis of eighteen focus groups conducted in 2025 in three countries that have been under increased scrutiny internationally due to their vulnerability to pro-Russian disinformation, but received limited attention in existing research: Poland, Romania and Serbia. Focusing on responses to examples of pro-Russian disinformation concerning the Russia-Ukraine war and LGBTQ+ rights, we show that participants judged claims not only based on credibility but also based on moral rightness, as well as engaged in contestations over the boundaries of legitimate controversy. Building on this evidence, we argue that disinformation not only creates uncertainty over how the world is but often invites contestation over how the world should be and over where the boundaries of legitimate public debate should lie. We conclude by reflecting on what these findings mean for scholarly research on disinformation, for counter-disinformation efforts, and for the way we understand the impact of disinformation on democracy.

articles.title: The Promise of Multistakeholderism: Transnational Influence and Legitimacy at the Internet Governance Forum
articles.abstract: Multistakeholderism is widely regarded as a means to ensure equal representation for stakeholders, promote democratic processes, and enable effective governance. Given the interconnected nature of the internet, much of global internet governance is influenced by multistakeholder approaches with a prominent role of transnational actors. This raises questions about the effects of transnational influence on the legitimacy of multistakeholder internet governance. Therefore, this article explores how transnational influence affects the input, throughput, and output legitimacy of the Internet Governance Forum (IGF), a key node within the internet governance ecosystem. The analysis combines qualitative content analysis of 600 statements made during cybersecurity governance debates at the IGF from 2016 to 2023 with 18 expert interviews. The findings reveal that transnational actors affect the IGF's legitimacy unevenly, producing both legitimacy gains and legitimacy deficits. Broad stakeholder participation contributes to high levels of input legitimacy, yet the prominence of specific transnational actors in panel discussions and policy contributions raises concerns regarding throughput legitimacy, reflecting persistent inequalities in access, resources, and visibility. While transnational actors' contributions significantly shape IGF policy outcomes, their influence is disproportionately concentrated among Global North actors. This article contributes to scholarship on transnational influence, the legitimacy of international organizations, and multistakeholderism.

articles.title: Governing for Digital Resilience: Rethinking Inclusion for WSIS+20 and Beyond
articles.authors: Audrey Yue, Jun Yu, Renae Sze Ming Loh
articles.abstract: At the WSIS+20 juncture, this article asks what conditions enable individuals to participate meaningfully in digital life, and how governance arrangements should be assessed accordingly. Multistakeholder governance has distributed authority across actors, but not necessarily the capacity to shape or respond to digital conditions. We argue that assessing this gap today requires attention to the different forms of power through which these conditions are produced, and to individuals' experiences as evidence of how those governance conditions operate in practice. Building on socio‐ecological resilience theory and the capabilities approach, we reconceptualise digital resilience not as an individual trait but as a process shaped by governance conditions and by the substantive freedom people have to adapt, recover, and participate over time. We then introduce the DRIVE (Digital Resilience Indicators for Veritable Empowerment) framework, an indicator‐based diagnostic architecture spanning six drivers and five levels—individual, familial, communal, platform, and state—that shifts assessment from individual preparedness towards enabling conditions. Using fraudulent advertising on Meta's platforms as an illustration, we show how DRIVE can identify evidenced constraints, evidence gaps, and appropriate sites of remedy. Rather than offering a universal score, DRIVE provides a flexible architecture for context‐specific assessment of the conditions under which digital resilience develops.

articles.title: Innovation and Competition on a Rugged Technological Landscape
articles.authors: Steven Callander, Nicolas S. Lambert, Niko Matouschek
articles.abstract: We integrate innovation into Hotelling's classic model of spatial competition. Potential entrants arrive sequentially and choose whether and where to innovate. They can innovate beyond the frontier, expanding the boundary of the market, or within a niche between incumbent products. Product quality is learned only after introduction, and uncertainty increases with novelty. Innovation on a rugged technological landscape is irregular, with frequent changes in direction and cycles between frontier and niche innovation. The ruggedness of the technological landscape itself deters innovation, generating fewer entrants, less product differentiation, narrower markets, and more intense competition than under certainty. (JEL D11, D21, D83, L11, L25, O31)

articles.title: Recurring Auctions with Costly Entry: Theory and Evidence
articles.abstract: Recurring auctions are widely used to sell durable assets, with follow-up auctions held for unsold items. We investigate such auctions theoretically and empirically. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that recurring auctions outperform single-round auctions when buyers face entry costs, enhancing efficiency and revenue due to sorted entry of potential buyers. Optimal reserve price sequences are characterized. Empirical findings from home foreclosure auctions in China reveal significant annual gains in efficiency (US$3.40 billion, 16.60 percent) and revenue (US$2.97 billion, 15.92 percent) using recurring auctions compared with single-round auctions. Implementing optimal reserve prices can further improve efficiency (3.35 percent) and revenue (3.06 percent). (JEL D44, D82, R31)

articles.title: Learning in the Marriage Market: The Economics of Dating
articles.authors: Yair Antler, Daniel Bird, Daniel Fershtman
articles.abstract: This paper develops a search-and-matching model where potential partners can learn about their compatibility as a couple by spending time together (interpreted as dating). We show that a steady-state equilibrium exists and characterize its induced dating patterns. In equilibrium, highly attractive individuals are more selective. We derive conditions under which equilibria induce positive assortative matching and show that even when these conditions hold, the socially optimal outcome can exhibit negative assortative matching. Finally, the framework is applied to study the effect of recent advances in search technologies on dating patterns and the connection between dating and interracial segregation. (JEL C78, D83, J12)

articles.title: Cognitive Ability and Perceived Disagreement in Learning
articles.abstract: Do agents believe they agree more with others over time? This paper explores how individuals perceive the belief-updating behavior of others and the resulting disagreement in a sequential experiment with public information. We uncover a persistent gap in the perception of disagreement as a function of cognitive ability. Higher cognitive ability correlates with less perceived disagreement, although the average subject underestimates the extent of actual disagreement. Information about a partner's cognitive ability only impacts perceived disagreement when the partner has a low test score. Our findings highlight the roles of overconfidence and cognitive projection in shaping these perceptions. (JEL C91, D12, D83, D91)

articles.title: Degree-Weighted Social Learning
articles.authors: Chen Cheng, Xiao Han, Xin Tong, Yusheng Wu, Yiqing Xing
articles.abstract: We study social learning in which agents weight neighbors' opinions differently based on their degrees, capturing situations in which agents place more trust in well-connected individuals or, conversely, discount their influence. We derive asymptotic properties of learning outcomes in large stochastic networks and analyze how the weighting rule affects societal wisdom and convergence speed. We find that assigning greater weight to higher-degree neighbors harms wisdom but has a non-monotonic effect on convergence speed, depending on the diversity of views within high- and low-degree groups, highlighting a potential trade-off between convergence speed and wisdom. (JEL D83, D85, Z13)

articles.title: Land, Wealth, and Taxation
articles.authors: Roberto Brunetti, Carl Gaigné, Fabien Moizeau
articles.abstract: This paper examines the role of land in wealth dynamics and its consequences for efficiency and inequality. We focus on the interplay among agents’ bidding for location, mortgage market imperfections, and inheritance in a model in which agents leave to their heirs financial bequests and their housing wealth. The borrowing constraint generates a housing return premium and spatial wealth sorting, which translate into persistent wealth inequality. Since altruism and the borrowing constraint distort land price formation, we show that taxing land rent transmitted between generations is optimal. Land taxation cannot be disconnected from taxation on intergenerational wealth transfers. (JEL D31, D64, H71, Q24, R23, R31, R52)

articles.title: Strategic Limit Orders and Intertemporal Price Dispersion
articles.authors: Suman Banerjee, Ravi Jagannathan, Kai Wang
articles.abstract: We study a two-period commodity market with competitive consumers and Cournot sellers. Without speculation, equilibrium is stationary. A storage-capable, strategically large speculator can profitably create deterministic intertemporal price dispersion using standard order types. A period-1 limit buy order flattens residual demand, induces higher output, and yields a low purchase price. With mandatory liquidation, resale remains below the no-speculation price but above the purchase price, so the speculator profits; consumers gain and sellers lose. With free disposal and a stop-loss, the period-2 price can exceed the benchmark, benefiting sellers but harming consumers. (JEL D43, G12, G14, G41, Q02)

articles.title: Electoral Campaign Attacks: Theory and Evidence
articles.abstract: This paper studies the determinants of electoral campaign attacks. We first propose a model to examine the main factors that influence candidates' decisions to attack. Our theoretical analysis yields a number of predictions that we test using information from “right of reply” lawsuits filed in Brazil. Our empirical analysis exploits a regression discontinuity design based on virtual ties between second- and third-place candidates to show that candidates with an electoral advantage are more likely to receive an attack. We then exploit another discontinuity to show that the patterns of campaign attacks differ significantly under single- and dual-ballot plurality systems. (JEL D72, D74, K16)

articles.title: Competitive Bottlenecks and Platform Spillovers
articles.abstract: We provide a general framework to analyze competition between oligopolistic platforms in competitive bottleneck settings, allowing for pricing and nonprice design choices by platforms, and post-participation buyer-seller decisions. We show that equilibrium choices by platforms are distorted against sellers’ interests in a way harmful to welfare (e.g., setting excessive commission fees), and that an increase in the number of competing platforms can exacerbate this distortion. We also characterize how buyer-side heterogeneity in interaction benefits, partial market coverage, platform asymmetry, and cross-platform spillovers further amplify or mitigate welfare distortions. Based on our findings, we discuss policy implications for mobile app platforms. (JEL D43, L13, L25, L96)

articles.title: Competing Diffusions in a Social Network
articles.authors: Arthur Campbell, C. Matthew Leister, Philip Ushchev, Yves Zenou
articles.abstract: We develop a model of competing diffusions of goods on a social network. There are two types of goods and individuals: mass-market and niche-market. There is a unique stable steady state, and the adoption of a mass-market good is greater than its population share. Greater connectivity and homophily will concurrently increase the prevalence of niche-market goods. If there is a strategic agent who wants to promote a niche good, she will invest more in influencing activities than one promoting mass-market goods. When individuals choose their degree of homophily, niche-market individuals exhibit greater homophily than mass-market ones. (JEL D83, D85, L86, Z13)

articles.title: Reputation and Competitive Selection
articles.abstract: We demonstrate how selection in competitive markets can impede long-run reputational incentives. In our model, competent firms can exert costly effort to improve expected product quality, but inept firms cannot. With low entry barriers, we show competent firms cannot persistently exert effort, despite bounded memory. Such effort would cause consumers to select firms based on reputations for competence, eventually selecting a monopolist with an arbitrarily high reputation, which has no incentive for effort. More generally, reputation-based selection rules out long-run effort, which undermines the basis for such selection. Intermediate entry barriers provide stronger reputational incentives than low or high barriers. (JEL D21, D40, D82, L15)

articles.title: The Perils of Overreaction
articles.abstract: To study updating rules, we consider the problem of a malevolent principal screening an imperfectly Bayesian agent. We uncover a fundamental dichotomy between underreaction and overreaction to information. If, for some signal realization, the agent's updating rule produces a posterior that lies outside the convex hull of the Bayesian posteriors induced by the signal structure, she can be exploited by the principal without bound: Her ex ante expected loss can be made arbitrarily large. In contrast, an agent who underreacts—whose posterior after each signal realization lies between the prior and the corresponding Bayesian posterior—cannot be exploited at all. (JEL D82, D83)

articles.title: Targeted Advertising in Elections
articles.abstract: How does targeted advertising influence electoral outcomes? This paper presents a one-dimensional spatial model of voting in which a privately informed challenger persuades voters to support him over the status quo. I show that targeted advertising enables the challenger to persuade voters with opposing preferences and swing elections decided by such voters. Ex ante commitment power is unnecessary—the challenger succeeds by strategically revealing different pieces of verifiable information to different voters. Publicizing all political ads would mitigate the negative effects of targeted advertising and help voters collectively make the right choice. (JEL D72, D82, D83, M37)

articles.title: Symmetric Equilibrium in Pre-auction Investment
articles.abstract: We characterize the symmetric equilibria of a pre-auction game of investment in an internet ad auction environment. For a wide class of auction formats, we show a symmetric equilibrium exists for the pre-auction investment game, is essentially unique, and is the same for all auction formats in the class. We give sufficient conditions for the symmetric equilibrium to be in pure strategies and to achieve the efficient level of investment. Finally, we show comparative statics results with respect to a variety of parameters. (JEL D44, D82)

articles.title: Optimal Procurement Design: A Reduced-Form Approach
articles.abstract: Standard procurement models assume that the buyer knows the quality of the good at the time of procurement; however, in many settings, the quality is learned only long after the transaction. We study procurement problems in which the buyer's valuation of the supplied good depends directly on its quality, which is unverifiable and unobservable to the buyer. For a broad class of procurement problems, we identify procurement mechanisms maximizing any weighted average of the buyer's expected payoff and social surplus. The optimal mechanism can be implemented via an auction that restricts sellers to submitting bids within specific intervals. (JEL D44, D82, H57, L15)

articles.title: Monopolistic Data Dumping
articles.abstract: A profit-maximizing monopolist curates a database for users seeking to learn a parameter. There are two user types: “Nowcasters” wish to learn the parameter's current value, while “forecasters” target its long-run value. Data storage involves a constant marginal cost. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts described by fees and data-access levels. The profit-maximizing menu offers full access to historical data, while current data are fully provided to nowcasters but may be withheld from forecasters. Compared to the social optimum, the monopolist keeps too much historical data, keeps too little current data, and may store too much data overall. (JEL C53, C80, D42, L12, L86)

articles.title: The Unintended Consequences of Academic Leniency
articles.authors: A. Brooks Bowden, Viviana Rodriguez, Zach Weingarten
articles.abstract: Education is widely recognized as the primary driver of human capital accumulation. However, policies designed to promote educational attainment often overlook students’ endogenous responses. This paper provides empirical evidence of the causal impact of relaxed academic standards on student effort and achievement. We find that academic leniency results in mechanical GPA increases, but significant reductions in effort among lower ability students based on lower attendance and lower numerical grades. These heterogeneous effects compound and exacerbate gaps in engagement and achievement throughout high school, ultimately worsening deficits in human capital accumulation as measured by ACT scores. (JEL H75, I21, I24, I28, J15)

articles.title: Childhood Health Shocks and the Intergenerational Transmission of Inequality
articles.authors: Tine M. Eriksen, Amanda P. Gaulke, Niels Skipper, Jannet Svensson, Peter R. Thingholm
articles.abstract: This paper documents a socioeconomic gradient in adult labor market penalties stemming from a single chronic and treatable childhood health shock in a country with universal access to health care. Using childhood onset type 1 diabetes, Danish administrative registry data, and causal forests, we estimate substantial variation in the employment and earnings penalties at age 30. These penalties vary systematically with parental income and maternal educational attainment. Our findings help explain the income-health gradient and have important implications for policy discussions related to the design of health care systems. (JEL H51, I12, I13, I18, J16, J23, J31)

articles.title: China’s Nationwide CO 2 Emissions Trading System: A General Equilibrium Assessment
articles.authors: Lawrence H. Goulder, Xianling Long, Chenfei Qu, Da Zhang
articles.abstract: China’s CO 2 emissions trading system, the world’s largest, aims to significantly reduce CO 2 emissions. The system is a tradable performance standard (TPS), differing from cap and trade (C&T). We provide a dynamic general equilibrium assessment that uniquely considers institutional and fiscal features of China that affect policy costs and distributional impacts. Key findings: The TPS’s environmental benefits exceed its costs by a factor of five or more. Interactions with the fiscal system reduce or eliminate the TPS’s cost disadvantage relative to C&T. Introducing auctioning as a complementary source of allowance supply can reduce costs by 30 percent. (JEL D58, O13, P28, Q54, Q58)

articles.title: The Role of Race in the Legal Representation of Low-Income Defendants
articles.abstract: Little is known about the role of race in the defense of low-income defendants by court-appointed attorneys. Exploiting the quasirandom assignment of court-appointed attorneys to cases, we test whether attorneys secure better deals for same-race defendants. Results indicate that while Black and White attorneys are similarly effective at representing White defendants, Black defendants who are represented by White rather than Black attorneys are 14–16 percent more likely to have their charges dismissed and 15–26 percent less likely to be incarcerated. Moreover, we find no evidence that having a different-race attorney increases the likelihood of reoffending in the future. (JEL H76, J15, K14, K42)

articles.title: The Effect of Deactivating Facebook and Instagram on Users’ Emotional State
articles.authors: Hunt Allcott, Matthew Gentzkow, Benjamin Wittenbrink, Winter Mason, Arjun Wilkins, Natalie Jomini Stroud, Joshua A. Tucker,
articles.abstract: We estimate the effect of social media deactivation on users’ emotional state in two large randomized experiments before the 2020 US election. People who deactivated Facebook for the six weeks before the election reported a 0.060 standard deviation improvement in an index of happiness, depression, and anxiety, relative to controls who deactivated for just the first of those six weeks. People who deactivated Instagram for those six weeks reported a 0.041 standard deviation improvement relative to controls. Exploratory analysis suggests that the Facebook effect is driven by people over 35, while the Instagram effect is driven by women under 25. (JEL D12, D91, I31, J16, L82)

articles.title: Identifying Tax Compliance from Variation in Tax Policy: Theory and Empirics
articles.authors: Andrew Bibler, Laura Grigolon, Keith F. Teltser, Mark J. Tremblay
articles.abstract: Governments increasingly use changes in tax rules to combat evasion. We develop a general approach to point-identify tax compliance along with supply and demand elasticities. Identification requires data on prices and quantities, variation in tax policy, and a demand or supply shifter. We illustrate our approach using data on Airbnb collection agreements, where taxes are enforced by shifting the statutory burden away from hosts and onto renters via the platform. We find that taxes are paid on roughly 0 to 1.6 percent of Airbnb transactions prior to enforcement. (JEL H25, H26, H71, K34, L83)

articles.title: Impacts of Corporate Tax Cuts on Firms and Workers: Evidence from Small Businesses
articles.abstract: This paper assesses the effects of corporate tax cuts on small firms and their workers. Following a reform in Quebec, Canada, firms receiving tax cuts expand and their workers’ earnings increase compared to workers and firms without tax cuts. We estimate that overall workers bear 35 percent of the tax burden, with larger incidence falling on those with ownership in the companies they work at, through increased profits. Additionally, workers across each tercile of the within-firm earnings distribution benefit from tax cuts, possibly because fair-wage concerns matter when after-tax profits rise due to close interactions among workers in small corporate environments. (JEL D22, H22, H25, J31, L25)

articles.title: Prioritizing Benefit? How Low-Income Patients Respond to Prescription Cost Sharing
articles.abstract: This paper measures how cost sharing impacts older low-income patients, exploiting a discontinuity in eligibility for a prescription drug subsidy for those who lose access to the Medicaid-linked program. Higher drug prices resulting from subsidy loss lead to a 40 percent reduction in prescription expenditures, driven by a 16 percent quantity reduction of prescriptions filled. Patients economize on purchases of higher-priced drugs, irrespective of their health benefits. For example, patients reduce insulin purchases by 35 percent. There is no evidence that cost sharing prompts switching from branded drugs to generics. This behavior suggests that cost sharing reduces prescription accessibility without enhancing cost-effectiveness. (JEL D24, I11, I18, I32, I38, L65)

articles.title: Can You Erase the Mark of a Criminal Record? Labor Market Impacts of Criminal Record Remediation
articles.authors: Amanda Agan, Andrew Garin, Dmitri Koustas, Alexandre Mas, Crystal S. Yang
articles.abstract: We investigate whether removing a previously obtained criminal record improves employment outcomes. We estimate the causal impact of criminal record remediation laws that have been widely enacted with the goal of improving employment opportunities for millions of individuals with records. We find consistent evidence that removing an existing record does not improve labor market outcomes, on average. A notable exception is participation in gig work through online platforms, which often screen workers based on their records but not their employment histories. The evidence is consistent with records initially scarring labor market trajectories in a way that is difficult to undo later. (JEL H76, J22, J23, K14, K42, M51)

articles.title: A Matter of Time? Measuring Effects of Public Schooling Expansions on Families
articles.authors: Chloe R. Gibbs, Jocelyn Wikle, Riley Wilson
articles.abstract: We leverage pronounced changes in the availability of public schooling for young children—through duration expansions to the kindergarten day—to better understand how an implicit childcare subsidy affects mothers and families. Exploiting full-day kindergarten variation across place and time from 1992 through 2022 and novel data on state-level policy changes, combined with a comparison of children of typical kindergarten-age to older children, we measure effects on parental labor supply and family childcare expenses. Full-day kindergarten expansions were responsible for as much as 24 percent of the growth in employment of mothers with kindergarten-age children in this time frame. (JEL H75, I21, J12, J13, J16, J22)

articles.title: How Effective Are R&D Tax Incentives? Reconciling the Micro and Macro Evidence
articles.authors: Silvia Appelt, Matěj Bajgar, Chiara Criscuolo, Fernando Galindo-Rueda
articles.abstract: Recent firm-level studies find R&D tax incentives to be much more effective at stimulating firms’ R&D investment than aggregate analyses suggest. Based on a distributed analysis of official R&D survey and administrative tax relief microdata for 19 OECD countries, we show that two factors can reconcile these contrasting results. First, the limited uptake of R&D tax incentives in most countries makes aggregate studies underestimate the effectiveness of R&D tax incentives. Secondly, R&D tax incentives are (much) less effective for large and R&D-intensive firms, which account for a small share of R&D-performing firms but most aggregate R&D tax relief. (JEL D22, H25, H32, L25, O31)

articles.title: The Pass-Through of Retail Crime
articles.abstract: This paper shows retailers increase prices in response to organized retail crime. We match store-level crime data to scanner data from the universe of transactions for cannabis retailers in Washington state. Using quasi-experimental variation from robberies and burglaries, we find a 1.7–1.8 percent price increase at victimized stores and nearby competitors. This rise is not driven by short-to-medium-term demand changes but is consistent with crime-related cost shocks. Effects are larger for independent stores and less concentrated markets. We estimate crime imposes a 1 percent “hidden” unit tax on affected stores, implying $30.7 million in additional social costs, primarily borne by consumers. (JEL D22, H22, H76, K42, L81)

articles.title: Trade Protection along Supply Chains
articles.authors: Chad P. Bown, Paola Conconi, Aksel Erbahar, Lorenzo Trimarchi
articles.abstract: We study the effects of trade protection along supply chains. We focus on temporary trade barriers against China, which has been the main target of US trade protection during the last decades. To deal with endogeneity concerns, we use an instrumental variable strategy, exploiting changes in the identity of swing states across presidential terms and heterogeneous exposure to these political shocks across industries. We find that politically motivated trade protection generates winners and losers: It fosters employment growth in protected industries but hampers employment growth in downstream industries. Our estimates imply a negative overall impact on US jobs. (JEL D72, F13, F14, L14, O19, P33)

articles.title: Polluted IPOs
articles.authors: Meng Miao, Wei Wang, Zhengyu Zuo
articles.abstract: Chinese companies must undergo a review by a regulator-appointed committee before proceeding with initial public offerings (IPOs). We find that firms—particularly, politically unconnected ones—are more likely to pass this review on polluted days (i.e., with a high level of PM2.5). The effect appears driven by reduced cognitive capacity among reviewers, reflected in fewer and simpler questions raised during review sessions. Notably, firms approved on polluted days show no significant performance difference from other firms within three years after the IPO. The findings suggest that pollution-induced cognitive fatigue may paradoxically reduce distortions in a politically influenced approval process. (JEL D22, G24, G32, K22, P28, P31, Q52)

articles.title: Inclusive Teaching: Spotting Social Isolation in the Classroom
articles.authors: Sule Alan, Michela Carlana, Marinella Leone
articles.abstract: We evaluate an intervention aimed at addressing social isolation in classrooms. The treatment provides teachers with their students’ social networks and information on developmental risks associated with social exclusion. Using friendship data and incentive-compatible measures, we find that the intervention reduces social isolation and antisocial behavior but does not increase prosocial behavior. Lower antisocial behavior enhances economic efficiency, reflected in higher average student payoffs and reduced inequality. Our findings highlight the personal and communal benefits of addressing social exclusion and antisocial peer dynamics in schools. (JEL D91, I21, I24, I28, J13, Z13)

articles.title: On-Demand Assistance: Experimental Evidence from Indonesia
articles.authors: Rema Hanna, Benjamin A. Olken, Sudarno Sumarto, Achmad Maulana, Vivi Alatas, Elan Satriawan
articles.abstract: Given labor informality in developing countries, addressing employment shocks is challenging. We study Indonesia’s new approach for on-demand online applications for temporary cash assistance and online job training. Through 20 lotteries over two years, 11 million beneficiaries were selected. In nationwide representative surveys matched with administrative data, most beneficiaries report not receiving the assistance, with no detectable impact on employment or consumption. In contrast, survey data from applicants with working phones reveal high reported take-up and higher incomes. The results suggest that, while flexible, on-demand assistance has potential, design features that allow for flexibility could hinder receipt and, thus, impact. (JEL E21, E24, I38, J24, J46, O15)

articles.title: Do felon voting rules affect criminal prosecutions?
articles.abstract: Felon disenfranchisement laws can alter the composition of the electorate. Accordingly, we argue that in states with such laws, elected prosecutors may be tempted to assign felon status strategically. We test our argument using criminal case data from Virginia and leveraging a sudden policy change—unexpectedly announced by the Governor on April 22, 2016—enfranchising all felons upon completion of their prison or probation sentence. Using well-known racial differences in partisanship as a measure of likely political alignment, we show that the announcement corresponded to an increase in criminal charge severity and sentence length for defendants who were politically unaligned with their prosecutors, and a decrease for aligned defendants. Evidence suggests that these changes may have been partially motivated by partisan concerns in the lead-up to the 2016 federal elections.

articles.title: Polity size and women’s representation: evidence from two large-scale boundary reforms
articles.authors: Moa Frödin Gruneau, Jan Teorell, Kåre Vernby
articles.abstract: Do larger polities hinder gender parity in elected office? We theorize that when populations grow faster than elected assemblies, a “seat congestion” effect intensifies competition for nominations, enabling men candidates to crowd out women. We test this argument using two nationwide natural experiments: Swedish municipal amalgamations in 1952 and 1973 that abruptly increased electorates. We track the effects in newly digitized historical panel data. Where electorate-per-seat ratios rose, growth in women’s representation slowed. Decomposition analyses show that expanding councils only partially offsets congestion. By identifying polity size as a systematic brake on descriptive representation, the study adds a demographic dimension to debates on institutional design and points to an overlooked cost of increasing jurisdictional size.

articles.title: “Manifestly unlawful”: How US troops think about the duty to disobey illegal orders
articles.authors: Charli Carpenter, Heather Kumove, Geraldine Santoso
articles.abstract: US troops are required to disobey unlawful orders but obey lawful ones – yet social scientists know very little about how they draw that line or what drives the decision to actually disobey when it counts. We asked 818 active-duty American troops to define “manifestly unlawful orders” in their own words, as well as whether they would obey or disobey specific scenarios in which they might be asked to directly and intentionally target unarmed civilians. A majority of troops could provide clear examples of situations in which they would feel compelled to disobey orders. Of specific scenarios, over a third of US troops were prepared to disobey orders to target civilians, either with nuclear weapons or if asked to shoot civilian protesters. Controlling for gender, age, branch of service, party affiliation, voting behavior, rank, income, and education, we find simply thinking ahead about the concept of “manifestly unlawful orders” is the single biggest predictor of soldiers’ willingness to refuse to harm civilians.

articles.title: Worth a try? The electoral consequences of symbolic legislation
articles.authors: Nicole Huffman, John V. Kane, David L. Stack
articles.abstract: With the US Congress increasingly gridlocked, fewer bills are becoming law. Nevertheless, members continue to engage in what we call “symbolic legislating”—that is, introducing legislation that has effectively no chance of securing enough votes to become law. Despite its prevalence, little is known about the electoral implications of sponsoring symbolic legislation. It is possible that voters reward their legislator’s efforts to move the status quo closer to their position even if it has no chance of becoming law. On the other hand, because symbolic legislation is doomed to fail, it may decrease a legislator’s perceived effectiveness and, thus, their political support. Alternatively, it is possible that sponsoring symbolic legislation has no impact beyond a cue of the politician’s position. In this Research Article, we test these competing hypotheses using a survey experiment. Our experimental results clearly demonstrate that, assuming shared party and issue position, sponsoring symbolic legislation is strongly rewarded. Moreover, the effect is even stronger among voters who are most likely to attend to this information in the real world and operates similarly across parties.

articles.title: Exploring the Predictors and Outcomes of Perceived Algorithm Responsiveness in Social Media Feeds: Combining Longitudinal and Computational Methods
articles.authors: Samuel Hardman Taylor, David M. Markowitz
articles.abstract: Perceptions of how algorithms curate content are integral to how people use social media and its effects. Building on the algorithm responsiveness process, we explore whether perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR) was associated with the message cues of algorithmically curated content. We coupled longitudinal data from a 7-day, twice-daily diary survey with computational digital traces from Twitter (now X) to operationalize algorithmic message characteristics and to understand the antecedents and outcomes of PAR ( N = 10,337 tweets). Results suggested that message cues from algorithmic content in social feeds (i.e., closeness, popularity, valence, and format) were associated with perceived message personalization, but message personalization was the only message characteristic associated with PAR. PAR predicted feeling more connected to others on Twitter, along with message-level factors: closeness to the poster and message personalization. This work contributes to the algorithm responsiveness process, demonstrating that characteristics of algorithmically curated messages predict how individuals experience algorithms.

articles.title: Do Experts Agree About Misinformation? Evidence From Three Annual Surveys
articles.authors: Sacha Altay, Sebastián Valenzuela, Philip N. Howard
articles.abstract: How much do experts on the information environment agree about the scale, spread, and effects of misinformation? We drew on three annual waves of the International Panel on the Information Environment expert survey to examine agreement with seven popular claims about misinformation (2023: N = 262; 2024: N = 413; 2025: N = 442; spanning 76 countries). Agreement varied widely across statements and was stable across waves. About 60% of experts agreed that falsehoods spread faster than the truth and that misinformation is widespread. About half agreed that misinformation has a substantial influence on behavior and that people readily believe what they see online; about 40% agreed that more people have become misinformed over time; and only 25% agreed that misinformation is primarily a social media problem. The surveys also revealed a persistent divide between experts who saw misinformation as widespread and consequential and those more skeptical, with sharpest disagreement on its behavioral impact and increase over time. In 2025, some experts distinguished between misperception prevalence and misinformation severity. Overall agreement varied by respondent background: agreement was higher among experts on developing countries than those on developed countries, higher among STEM researchers than social scientists, and lower among political scientists than communication scholars. Expert consensus on misinformation is partial, varies across claims and experts, and is shaped by geography and discipline.

articles.title: Exclusion Forms Connection: The Presence of Immigrant Linked Fate Among Nonimmigrants
articles.authors: Yoshira D. Macías Mejía, Lisa M. Sanchez
articles.abstract: Immigrant linked fate is a new measure in the linked fate literature. In this study, we examine the predictors of immigrant linked fate, validate the measure of linked fate, and examine the role of immigrant linked fate in shaping immigration policy preferences among Latinos, Blacks, and Asians. We suggest that one must not be an immigrant to espouse immigrant linked fate. Therefore, “immigrant” linked fate has less to do with nativity and more to do with outsider status as the result of social exclusion. To test our hypotheses, we use the Collaborative Multiracial Post-Election Survey 2016 (CMPS) because it includes the measure of immigrant linked fate and a robust racial and ethnic group sample. The results suggest that Latinos, Blacks, and Asians have similar predictors of immigrant linked fate. We find immigrant linked fate is a distinct measure from racial linked fate and that immigrant linked fate predicts policy preferences.

articles.title: Measuring White Identity
articles.abstract: Scholars increasingly emphasize identity politics as a crucial factor influencing white political behavior, which is often conceptualized as a form of defensive solidarity. But does current measurement accurately capture this concept? This study reconsiders the measurement of white identity to more accurately reflect its conceptualization, distinguishing between identity and consciousness without imposing ideological interpretations of group membership. I develop and test adapted measures for white identity and consciousness, allowing for ideological variation, and find that existing measures disproportionately reflect whites who are racially conservative in part because of measurement. Testing the measures on support for Trump and affirmative action, I find that the effects of white identity are conditional on the ideological interpretation of group consciousness embedded in existing measures. This study challenges dominant assumptions about the inherent conservatism of white identity and contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of racial politics in the United States.

The ethical trilemma in refugee protection: equity, sovereignty, autonomy
articles.abstract: Disparities in the distribution of protection responsibilities are not just unequal but also highly inequitable. Such inequities can be expected to negatively impact both the scope and the quality of protection that states are willing to provide. The paper empirically demonstrates through the analysis of Europe’s responses to forced displacement from former Yugoslavia to Ukraine, that European states have struggled to effectively address the highly inequitable distribution of refugee responsibilities. EU policy makers find it easier to develop symbolic solidarity measures than to establish more substantive policy responses, i.e. they struggle to adopt the kind of cooperation that the public goods literature suggests is necessary to overcome collective action problems. This is due to the fact that substantive refugee solidarity initiatives, such as quota-based relocation, which are promising from an equity perspective pose fundamental challenges to both national sovereignty and the individual autonomy of protection seekers. How future EU policies will seek to address such solidarity dilemmas that lie at the heart of international refugee responsibility sharing efforts will tell us much about its commitment to effective refugee protection.

articles.authors: Luke Rosedahl, Yuka Sasaki, Takeo Watanabe
articles.abstract: Categorization is crucial for survival, helping animals forage, navigate, and avoid predators—all tasks involving movement. Yet, dominant theories of category learning treat it as a purely cognitive or perceptual process. Here, we challenge this view by demonstrating that physical movement can enhance category learning—but selectively. Using immersive virtual reality, we found that performing large actions, such as swinging a lightsaber, substantially improved learning of categories requiring integration of multiple cues (e.g., distinguishing aggressive from noncancerous lesions), while having minimal impact on categories involving independent evaluation of features (e.g., sorting by color and shape). This selective enhancement reveals a previously unrecognized motor contribution to categorization and may explain why prior studies missed it, opening avenues for optimizing training in critical categorization tasks.

articles.abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.
